title: Pastel
text: Pastel A modern cross platform app framework and toolchain for Object Pascal. Write your app once in Object Pascal and run it on the desktop, on servers and on Raspberry Pi — and, next, on Android phones. Pastel is built on top of the Free Pascal https://www.freepascal.org/ compiler and brings a modern developer experience: a simple command line tool, clear project conventions, forms with hot reload, and a UI drawn by Pastel itself so it looks the same everywhere. Status: 1.0 release candidate. Working today: the pastel command line tool and libraries for console programs on Linux, Windows and Raspberry Pi arguments, files, HTTP, JSON, settings, logging, tests, packaging , Linux services and REST APIs web server, JWT and API keys, SQLite/PostgreSQL/MySQL with migrations, background workers, .deb and Docker packages , and code intelligence in VS Code completion, hover, parameter hints, references, rename, compiler errors while typing and desktop apps on Linux and Windows forms from .pform files designed in VS Code, about 30 controls including grids and trees, your own controls in the designer, data binding, menus and shortcuts, dialogs, several windows, translations, themes, high DPI, hot reload, scripted UI tests; Windows installer, AppImage and .deb packages . Ideas, feedback and contributions are very welcome. Why Pastel? Object Pascal is a fast, readable, compiled language with a loyal community. But today you have two choices: Delphi is powerful and modern, but commercial. Lazarus is free and open source, but its IDE and workflow feel dated, and mobile support is limited. Pastel aims to be the missing piece: free, open source, modern, and easy to set up. Goals One codebase, many platforms: Linux, Windows and Raspberry Pi today; Android as a preview docs/android.md docs/android.md ; macOS and iOS are open for contributions ROADMAP.md open for contributions Any kind of app: GUI apps, terminal tools, servers and headless device programs Easy setup: pastel doctor finds and installs missing compilers and SDKs Modern editor experience: VS Code extension with code completion, live preview and hot reload Clear conventions: every Pastel project has the same structure, so you always know where things are Familiar for Pascal developers: components, properties and events, the way Delphi developers already think Try it today New here? Start with docs/getting started.md docs/getting started.md : from installing to a packaged program in fifteen minutes. All the documentation docs/README.md is ordered by topic, with examples on every page: guides that build a whole program step by step, every control docs/controls.md and every command docs/commands.md with an example, and examples/ examples with complete programs. You need Free Pascal https://www.freepascal.org/ 3.2 or newer on Linux Mint / Ubuntu: sudo apt install fpc fpc source . GUI apps also use SDL2 and FreeType, which most Linux desktops already have sudo apt install libsdl2 2.0 0 libfreetype6 ; Windows programs get SDL2.dll and freetype.dll next to them automatically. Install a release Linux : download it from the Releases page and run its install.sh , or unpack the archive and put its bin/ on your PATH . On Windows, unpack the .zip . In VS Code, install the Pastel extension. Or build it from the sources: This creates bin/pastel . Put it on your PATH for example ln s "$PWD/bin/pastel" ~/.local/bin/pastel , then create a desktop app: Or a console program arguments, help , colors, tables and questions are ready to use; see docs/console.md docs/console.md , docs/data.md docs/data.md for JSON, settings and logging, and docs/system.md docs/system.md for files, other programs and HTTP : Build output goes to build/<platform /<debug release / . Compiler errors point to the file and line, relative to your project. Building for another platform needs Free Pascal's units for it. pastel doctor tells you what is missing. title: Getting started
text: Getting started From nothing to a program you can hand out, in about fifteen minutes. The commands are for Linux Mint, Ubuntu, Debian ; Windows differences are noted. 1. Install Free Pascal Pastel uses the Free Pascal compiler 3.2 or newer and does not change it. Linux Mint / Ubuntu / Debian: sudo apt install fpc Windows: the installer from freepascal.org https://www.freepascal.org/download.html choose the 64 bit Windows version , and say yes to adding it to PATH . Check: fpc iV prints 3.2.2 or newer . 2. Build the pastel tool This makes bin/pastel bin\pastel.exe . Put it on your PATH so you can type pastel anywhere: On Windows: Settings → System → About → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables , and add the bin folder to Path . Then: It checks the compiler, the libraries for desktop apps and HTTPS, and which platforms this computer can build for. Every ✗ comes with the command that fixes it. 3. Install the VS Code extension In VS Code: Extensions Ctrl+Shift+X → … menu → Install from VSIX… → vscode/pastel vscode <version .vsix . For debugging F5 , VS Code also needs Microsoft's C/C++ extension; Pastel offers to install it the first time you press F5. 4. Your first program or in VS Code: Pastel: New Project from the command palette, Ctrl+Shift+P. The project looks like this; every Pastel project has the same layout: Press F9 or click ▶ Pastel Run in the status bar . The program is compiled and runs in the terminal panel: It already understands arguments: pastel run help , pastel run Ali , pastel run shout Ayşe . 5. Change it, and see it at once Run Pastel: Run and Watch or pastel run watch in a terminal . Now every time you save, the program is compiled and started again. Change the greeting in src/services/greeting.pas , press Ctrl+S, and look at the terminal. Mistakes show up in the Problems panel with the line; click to jump there. When you save a .pas file it is also formatted indentation, spaces . If you prefer to do that yourself, remove "editor.formatOnSave" from .vscode/settings.json ; pastel fmt formats everything at once. 6. Test Open the Testing view the flask icon on the left . It lists the tests in tests/ . Click ▶ to run them; a failing test is marked at the line of the assert that failed. In a terminal: pastel test . A test is a published method of a TTestSuite class: More in testing.md testing.md . 7. Debug Click left of a line number in src/main.pas to set a breakpoint, then press F5 . Pastel builds the program and starts it in the debugger; it stops at the breakpoint. Hover over a variable to see its value, and use the buttons at the top to step through the code. Values are shown readably: strings as text 'Ayşe' , objects as their real class with their properties, lists with their items TStringList 2 = {'elma', 'şeftali'} , JSON as JSON TJSONObject {"name": "Ayşe", "age": 30} . No launch.json is needed. To give your program arguments while debugging, add "args": "Ali" to the configuration in .vscode/launch.json . 8. Release makes dist/hello 0.1.0 linux.tar.gz : an optimized build with your README, ready to hand out and a .sha256 file to check the download . Change version in pastel.toml for the next release; hello version follows. For Windows and the Raspberry Pi: Building for another platform needs the Free Pascal cross compiler for it. pastel doctor shows which ones are ready; today fpcupdeluxe https://github.com/LongDirtyAnimAlf/fpcupdeluxe is the easiest way to add them. 9. A desktop app In VS Code: Pastel: New Project… or New Project on the Welcome page → Desktop → Desktop App , a name and a folder; the project opens with its form in the designer. Or in a terminal: A window opens. Open src/forms/Home.pform in VS Code: the form designer appears beside the editor. Change a text, drag a button: the running window follows at once. The code for the buttons is in src/forms/Home.pas ; F12 switches between form and code. See forms.md forms.md . Where next guide cli.md g

title: The Pastel Handbook
text: The Pastel Handbook Object Pascal from your first line to your first app — on computers and phones. This handbook teaches two things together: the Object Pascal language , from the beginning to an intermediate level, and Pastel , the toolkit that turns Pascal programs into command line tools, desktop apps and Android apps. You need no earlier Pascal. If you have written some code in another language, the first chapters will go quickly; if this is your first language, take them slowly and do the exercises. Every chapter builds on the one before, and the whole book builds one program: Pocket , a small money tracker. You write down what you spend and earn; Pocket tells you where the money goes. It starts as a few lines on the command line and ends as an app with a database, charts, PDF reports, two languages and an Android package. ! Pocket at the end of the book images/pocket.png Every complete program in this book is compiled and run whenever Pastel changes, and its output is checked against what the book says it prints tests/handbook.py . title: 1. Your first program
text: 1. Your first program In this chapter you write a program, run it, and learn what each of its lines means. Pascal, Object Pascal, Free Pascal, Pastel Pascal was designed in 1970 by Niklaus Wirth to teach programming: its code reads almost like English, and the compiler catches many mistakes before the program ever runs. Turbo Pascal made it fast and popular in the 1980s; Delphi 1995 added objects and visual forms, and the language became Object Pascal . Free Pascal is a free compiler for it that makes programs for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and more. Pastel is built on Free Pascal. It adds what a modern program needs — a project file, a command that builds, tests and packages, a library of units for files, JSON, HTTP, databases, and forms that look the same on every platform — so you can write the program and let Pastel deal with the rest. Programs written in Object Pascal are compiled into machine code: they start at once, run fast, and need nothing installed to run — not even Pastel. A project Open a terminal or VS Code's: Terminal → New Terminal and type: pastel new console made a folder with a small command line program; pastel run compiled it and ran it. In VS Code, Pastel: New Project… does the same, and F9 runs the project. The folder holds: For the first chapters you only need src/main.pas . Open it, delete everything, and type this: Run it with pastel run or F9 : Line by line program Hello; names the program. The name follows the rules of every name in Pascal: letters, digits and , starting with a letter. The semicolon ends the line's statement. {$mode objfpc}{$H+} are compiler directives : settings for the compiler, written as comments that start with $ . {$mode objfpc} chooses Free Pascal's object oriented dialect, the one this book uses. {$H+} makes string a modern string of any length. Put both lines at the top of every program and unit; pastel new does it for you. begin … end. hold what the program does. The last end of a program has a full stop, not a semicolon: it is the end of the file as far as the compiler cares. WriteLn 'Hello, world!' ; writes a line on the screen. Text in Pascal goes between single quotes. To write a quote itself, write it twice: 'It''s fine' . Case does not matter Pascal does not care about upper and lower case: WriteLn , writeln and WRITELN are the same. Pastel's code and this book write names with capitals WriteLn , PocketMoney and keywords in lower case begin , end — the way most Pascal code looks. pastel fmt puts the keywords right for you. Semicolons separate A semicolon separates one statement from the next. The statement before an end does not need one, but it does no harm, and adding the next line is easier when it is there: Writing more than text WriteLn writes several things one after the other, separated by commas. Write does the same without ending the line: Reading what the user types ReadLn waits until the user types a line and presses Enter. To keep what was typed you need a variable , a named place for a value. Variables are declared in a var section before begin — chapter 2 explains them; here is a first one: When the user types Ayşe : On the screen the answer appears after the question, where it was typed. Comments The compiler skips comments. Pascal has three kinds: Write comments that say why , not what: Inc Total, Price needs no comment, but the reason an unusual line is there does. When something is wrong Make a mistake on purpose: delete the semicolon after WriteLn 'one' in the program Three and run it. The compiler gives the file, the line and column 7,3 , and what it expected. It found the problem at the start of line 7 — the place right after the missing semicolon. Messages often point just after the real mistake: look at the line before, too. In VS Code the mistake is underlined as you type, and Problems Ctrl+Shift+M lists them all. Building without running A debug build carries what the debugger needs and checks more an array index outsi

title: 2. Values, types and variables
text: 2. Values, types and variables A program works with values: numbers, text, true or false. In Pascal every value has a type , and the compiler checks that types fit together before the program runs. This catches many mistakes early — adding a word to a number, or putting a fraction where only whole numbers belong. Variables A variable is a named place for a value. You declare it in a var section, with its type, before the begin that uses it; then := puts a value into it: Remember the two signs: := puts a value into a variable , = compares if Count = 3 then … . Several variables of one type can share a line: A, B, C: Integer; . Give variables names that say what they hold — Total , CustomerName , IsPaid — not x or tmp . Code is read far more often than it is written. A variable inside a procedure chapter 4 has no value until you give it one. The compiler warns you when you use one too early: read the warnings, they are usually right. Whole numbers Type Holds Integer −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 the everyday whole number Int64 about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ big counts, ids, file sizes Byte 0 to 255 one byte of a file, a color channel Word 0 to 65,535 a year, a month Cardinal 0 to 4,294,967,295 only positive Low and High tell the smallest and biggest value of a type: Arithmetic div divides whole numbers and drops the rest; mod gives the rest. / always gives a real number, even for 6 / 3 — so the compiler refuses A := 6 / 3 when A is an Integer . Multiplication and division go before addition and subtraction; brackets change the order. Real numbers Double holds numbers with a fraction: 3.14 , 0.001 , 2.5e6 −2.5 million . It is fast and precise to about 15 digits — but it stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly: FloatToStr rounds what it shows, so D looks like 0.3 — but it is 0.30000000000000004, and the comparison says so. For money use Currency : it keeps exactly four decimal places, so cents never drift. Pocket keeps every amount as a Currency . Two more surprises in that output: Round rounds a half to the even number 2.5 → 2, 3.5 → 4: "banker's rounding", which keeps sums of many rounded numbers fair , and Trunc just cuts the fraction off. True or false A Boolean is True or False . Comparisons make them, and and , or , not combine them: The brackets are needed. and binds stronger than = , so Age = 18 and HasTicket means Age = 18 and HasTicket — the compiler refuses it. Put brackets around every comparison you combine. Letters and text A Char is one character 'A' , a string is text of any length. + joins strings: Chapter 6 is about text: it has more to say, especially about letters like ş and ü . Constants A value that never changes gets a name in a const section. The name says what the number means, and changing it later is one edit instead of many: From one type to another Pascal does not change types behind your back: an Integer does not become a string by itself. The SysUtils unit has the functions that convert add uses SysUtils; after the directives, as in the program above : From To IntToStr 42 '42' StrToInt '42' 42 an exception chapter 9 when it is not a number StrToIntDef 'x', 0 0 a default instead TryStrToInt '42', N True , N = 42 the safe way for user input FloatToStr 2.5 '2.5' CurrToStr Price '4.5' Round 2.7 , Trunc 2.7 3 , 2 real to whole Ord 'A' , Chr 65 65 , 'A' a character's number and back An Integer becomes a Double by itself where one is needed no value is lost ; the other way needs Round or Trunc . Format Format builds text from a pattern and values, and controls how numbers look: %s is a string, %d a whole number, %f a real number %.2f : two decimals , %% a percent sign. A number before the letter is the width %5d , a minus aligns to the left. The values go between . Format writes numbers the computer's way when it has a FormatSettings that says so; Pastel programs write a dot unless told otherwise. Chapter 19 shows numbers in the user's language. In P

title: 3. Decisions and loops
text: 3. Decisions and loops A program that always does the same thing is not much use. This chapter makes programs choose if , case and repeat for , while , repeat . if No semicolon before else . if … then A else B is one statement; a semicolon after A would end it, and the else would stand alone — the compiler stops there. Several statements: begin … end then and else take one statement. For more, put them between begin and end — a compound statement : else if Choices in a row are written as a chain: The first condition that holds wins; the others are not even looked at. case When one value decides between many choices, case is clearer than a chain of if s. It works for whole numbers, characters, enumerations chapter 5 and — in Free Pascal — strings: 1..5 is a range, 6, 7 a list. The else part runs when nothing matched; without it, nothing happens. Every case ends with its own end . for for repeats a statement for every number from one value to another: to counts up, downto down. The loop variable must be a local variable of a whole number type or a Char , or an enumeration ; do not change it inside the loop, and do not rely on its value after the loop ends — the compiler does not promise what it is. Loops can be inside each other: while and repeat for is for a known number of times. When the loop goes on until something happens , use while or repeat : while checks before each round, so its body may never run. repeat … until checks after , so the body runs at least once — the natural form for "ask until the answer is right": repeat and until hold several statements without begin / end . Note that until takes the condition to stop , while the condition to go on . Break and Continue Break leaves the loop at once; Continue skips to the next round: In Pocket A first look at what Pocket will do: the expenses of a week, the days over a daily budget, the total. The amounts are written straight into the program here; chapter 5 keeps them in an array. Exercises 1. Print the numbers from 1 to 30, but Fizz for those divisible by 3, Buzz for 5, and FizzBuzz for both. 2. Ask for a month number and print how many days it has ignore leap years with one case . 3. Print a triangle of stars, five lines, one star more on each line. 4. ★ The computer "thinks" of a number from 1 to 100 Randomize; Secret := Random 100 + 1; . Let the user guess, and say "higher" or "lower" until it is right; then say how many guesses it took. Next: 4. Procedures and functions 04 routines.md

title: 4. Procedures and functions
text: 4. Procedures and functions As a program grows, the same steps come back in several places, and the main block gets long. Procedures and functions give a group of statements a name: you write it once and call it wherever it is needed. Together they are called routines . A procedure A routine is declared before the begin of the program, after the var and const sections — and before the code that calls it: Pascal reads from top to bottom. Parameters Values given to a routine are its parameters ; they are declared in brackets with their types: I is a local variable of Rule : it exists while Rule runs and nobody else sees it. Each call has its own. A function A function gives back a value. Inside it, Result is that value: A function call is a value, so it can stand wherever a value of its type can — in WriteLn , in a sum, inside another call. Exit Exit leaves a routine at once. In a function, Exit Value sets Result and leaves — handy for the simple cases first: How parameters are passed Written The routine gets Use it for X: Integer a copy; changing it changes only the copy small values the routine may change for itself const X: string the value, which it may not change strings, records, arrays: no copy is made — faster var X: Integer the caller's variable itself giving back more than one value, changing the caller's out X: Integer the caller's variable, to fill answers only its old value is not looked at A var or out parameter needs a variable when called: TwiceVar 5 does not compile 5 is not a place that can change . Use const for strings you only read — it is the habit of Pascal programmers, and of Pastel's own code. The TryStrToInt S, N you met in chapter 2 is such a function: it gives back True or False , and the number through its out parameter. Default values A parameter with a default may be left out when calling: Parameters with defaults come last. Overloading Several routines can share a name when their parameters differ; the compiler picks the one that fits: overload is optional in {$mode objfpc} ; it is needed in {$mode delphi} , so writing it keeps code portable. Routines inside routines A routine can have routines of its own, declared before its begin . They see its parameters and local variables, and nobody else sees them: A routine that calls itself A function may call itself — recursion . Each call has its own parameters, and one case must stop it: Recursion fits things that are built of smaller things of the same kind: folders in folders, a tree of menu items. For simple counting, a loop is clearer. In Pocket Pocket writes amounts in one way everywhere: two decimals, a comma between thousands — 1,234.50 . That is a job for a function. A first version chapter 6 makes it handle negative amounts too, and chapter 7 moves it into a unit of its own : Why not Round ? Chapter 2 showed that Round rounds a half to the even number: half a cent would sometimes go up and sometimes down. Adding 0.5 and cutting the rest Trunc always goes up. %.2d writes a whole number with at least two digits: 5 becomes 05 . Exercises 1. Write function Max3 A, B, C: Integer : Integer and test it with a few numbers. 2. Write procedure Swap var A, B: Integer that exchanges two variables. 3. Write a function IsLeapYear Year: Integer : Boolean divisible by 4, but not by 100 unless also by 400 . Check it against SysUtils.IsLeapYear . 4. ★ Write a recursive function Power Base: Double; Exponent: Integer : Double that works for negative exponents too. Next: 5. Arrays, records, enumerations and sets 05 structured types.md

title: 5. Arrays, records, enumerations and sets
text: 5. Arrays, records, enumerations and sets So far every variable held one value. Real data comes in groups: the expenses of a month, the parts of an address, the days a shop is open. This chapter shows Pascal's ways of building types out of other types. New types are named in a type section, which comes before var : By custom, type names start with T . Arrays An array is a row of values of one type, reached by number. Fixed size array 1..7 says which numbers the elements have; Low and High give them back, so loops never go wrong when the range changes. A debug build stops the program with an error when an index is outside the range — a bug found early instead of strange values later. Dynamic arrays When the number of elements is known only while the program runs, use a dynamic array. It starts empty; SetLength gives it a size, and it always counts from 0: Length is the number of elements, High the last index Length 1 ; −1 when empty . The memory is freed by itself when the array is no longer used. for … in walks through every element without an index — use it whenever you do not need the index. Growing an array one element at a time is fine for tens or hundreds of elements. For many thousands, the lists of chapter 10 grow more cleverly. Array parameters and literals A parameter declared array of Integer takes any array of integers — fixed or dynamic — and also a list written in brackets: Inside such a routine the elements are numbered from 0, whatever the caller's array used. Records A record groups values of different types that belong together — one thing with several parts: Assigning a record copies it: the two variables are separate afterwards. Objects, in chapter 8, behave differently — remember this. TDateTime is how Pascal keeps a moment: a Double counting days since 30 December 1899, the fraction being the time of day. EncodeDate makes one, FormatDateTime writes it, Date is today and Now this moment. Enumerations An enumeration is a type with a fixed list of named values. Instead of a number or a string that "means" something, the meaning is in the type, and the compiler checks it: The values often get a short prefix ek for entry kind , so their names never clash with others. An array can be indexed by an enumeration: array TEntryKind of string has one element per kind — add a kind and the compiler reminds you of every such array that needs one more element. Ord gives the position from 0 , Succ and Pred the next and the previous value; enumerations work in for and case . Sets A set holds some of the values of an enumeration or of small numbers, or characters — each one is in it or not: in asks whether a value is in the set; + joins two sets, keeps what both have, takes away. A test like C in '0'..'9' is shorter and faster than four comparisons. In Pocket With these types, Pocket's data has a shape: an entry is a record, its kind an enumeration, and the month a dynamic array of entries. with List High List do lets the statements inside name the fields of that element directly. Use with only for short blocks like this one: in a long block it is hard to see which name belongs to what. List is a var parameter in Add the procedure changes the caller's array and a const one in Total only read, and not copied . Exercises 1. Keep the marks of a class in an array of Integer and print the average, the highest and the lowest. 2. Make a record TAddress street, city, postcode and a procedure that prints one on three lines. 3. Make an enumeration of the seasons and a function that gives the season of a month 1..12 with case . 4. ★ Add function ByCategory const List: TEntries; const Category: string : Currency to the Pocket program and print what was spent on Food . Next: 6. Text 06 strings.md

title: 6. Text
text: 6. Text Most programs spend much of their time with text: names, notes, file lines, messages. This chapter shows how Pascal keeps text, the routines that cut and search it, and the one thing that surprises everyone — letters like ş , é or € . Strings are UTF 8 bytes A string with {$H+} holds text of any length. Pastel programs keep it in UTF 8 , the encoding of the web and of Linux: English letters take one byte each, letters like ş or ü two, € three, an emoji four. Length counts bytes , and S I is the I th byte : Length says 5 for Ayşe : the ş is two bytes. CharCount from Pastel.Text counts the letters a person sees. UpperCase from SysUtils only knows the English letters a–z, so it leaves ş alone. Upper and Lower from Pastel.Text know every alphabet — and with 'tr' they follow Turkish, where i becomes İ . The rule of thumb: the routines below work on bytes, and that is fine for searching, cutting at a found position, splitting and joining — UTF 8 is built so that these never cut a letter in half by accident. Count letters with CharCount , cut by letters with CharCopy , and change case with Upper / Lower . The everyday routines Pos Sub, S where Sub starts in S from 1 ; 0 when it is not there Copy S, From, Count Count bytes from position From MaxInt for "the rest" Delete S, From, Count , Insert Sub, S, At change S itself Trim , TrimLeft , TrimRight without spaces and tabs, line breaks at the ends StringReplace S, Old, New, Flags rfReplaceAll for every one, rfIgnoreCase for any case SameText A, B , CompareText A, B compare without case English letters LowerCase , UpperCase English letters only — Lower , Upper for every language String helpers: Split, Join and friends Strings also have methods, written after a dot: Careful: the helpers count from 0 IndexOf says 10 where Pos would say 11 , the classic routines from 1. Split gives a TStringArray — a dynamic array of strings. Line breaks and special characters LineEnding the line break of the system 10 on Linux and Android, 13 10 on Windows 10 , 13 , 9 the characters with these numbers: line feed, carriage return, tab 'a' + 9 + 'b' characters join strings like text does Building text Joining strings with + in a loop is simple and fine for most uses: For long texts built from thousands of pieces, a TStringList chapter 10 or TStringBuilder is faster. In Pocket: reading an amount People type amounts in different ways: 12 , 12.5 , 12,50 , 1,234.50 , or — in many countries — 1.234,50 . Pocket accepts all of them. The rule: the last dot or comma with one or two digits after it starts the cents; other dots and commas only group thousands. Read it slowly — it uses nearly everything of this chapter and the ones before: S I in '.', ',' is a set test on one byte; digits, dots and commas are all one byte in UTF 8, so walking byte by byte is safe here: any other letter is simply "not a digit". DefaultFormatSettings holds the computer's way of writing numbers. A copy with a dot as the decimal separator makes TryStrToCurr read 12.5 the same on every computer. Each early Exit False handles one wrong case; the rest of the function only deals with good input. Exercises 1. Count the words in a sentence Split on spaces; skip empty parts . 2. Write function Initials const FullName: string : string — 'Ada King Lovelace' gives 'AKL' . 3. Reverse a word. Try it with Ayşe . What goes wrong when you reverse bytes, and how would CharCopy help? 4. ★ Write function IsValidEmail const S: string : Boolean : one @ , something before it, and a dot somewhere after it. It will not catch everything — no simple test does. Next: 7. Units 07 units.md
headings: String helpers: Split, Join and friends

title: 7. Units
text: 7. Units A program in one file is fine for a page of code. Beyond that, it gets hard to find things, and code that would be useful elsewhere is stuck inside it. Pascal splits programs into units : files of related types and routines, each with a public part and a private part. This chapter shows how units work — and starts Pocket for real. A unit A unit has two parts: interface — the declarations other code may use: types, constants, variables, and the first line of each public routine. It is the unit's promise to the rest of the program. implementation — the code of those routines, and anything else the unit needs only for itself Polite here: nobody outside can call it . The unit ends with end. The file is named after the unit, in lower case: greetings.pas . A program or another unit names the unit in its uses clause, and from then on can use what its interface offers: Two uses clauses A unit can have a uses clause in each part. Units needed by the interface a type used in a public declaration go in the first; units needed only by the code go in the implementation one. Keep the first short: everything it names becomes a dependency of everyone who uses your unit. Two units may not use each other in their interface parts — Pascal needs to know one before the other. When two units really need each other, one of them names the other in its implementation's uses . Names from two units When two units offer the same name, the unit named later in uses wins. To pick one, write the unit's name before it: SysUtils.Format ... , Greetings.Greet ... . initialization and finalization A unit may end with code that runs once when the program starts, and once when it ends: The initialization of every unit runs before the program's begin , in the order of the uses clauses. A finalization section, after it, runs when the program ends — the place to free what the initialization made chapter 8 shows freeing . By then the screen may already be closed, so do not write to it there. Use them sparingly: code that runs "by itself" is easy to forget about. Where units live in a Pastel project Pastel finds the units of a project by itself: every .pas file in src/ and its sub folders. There is no list to keep up to date — make a file, name the unit in uses , and build. A common layout: The folders are for people; to the compiler a unit is a unit, wherever it is. pastel new also gives every project a unit you do not see: AppInfo , made from pastel.toml at every build. AppName and AppVersion in it always match the project file. Pocket begins Time to start the real program. Make a project: Pocket's first unit is everything about money as text: writing an amount FormatMoney , chapter 4 and reading one TryParseMoney , chapter 6 . Make src/pocketmoney.pas : <! file: examples/pocket core/src/pocketmoney.pas Some things are new since the versions in chapters 4 and 6: The comment at the top says what the unit is for, with an example. Write one for every unit: it is the first thing a reader sees. The interface has only the two routines and a comment for each — the contract. How they do it is in the implementation, which a user of the unit never needs to read. FormatMoney handles negative amounts: it remembers the sign, works on the positive amount, and puts the minus back at the end. Now src/main.pas uses it: repeat … until False loops forever; the Break inside is the way out. An empty input — the line after 4 — ends it. The program is short because the details live in the unit. That is the point: main.pas says what happens, the units say how . Exercises 1. Move the Week program's day names chapter 5 into a unit Days with a function DayName Day: Integer : string , and use it from a program. 2. Give PocketMoney a function FormatMoneyWith Amount: Currency; const Symbol: string : string that writes '12.50 €' . Use FormatMoney inside it. 3. What happens when a program uses a unit that is not in src/ ? Read the compiler's message. 4. ★ Make two un

title: 8. Classes and objects
text: 8. Classes and objects A record keeps data together. A class keeps data together with the code that works on it , and decides which parts the rest of the program may touch. Classes are the "Object" in Object Pascal; forms, controls, lists, database connections — nearly everything in Pastel is one. A first class Step by step: Fields hold the data. By custom their names start with F . Methods are the routines of the class, declared in it and written below with the class name in front: TAccount.Deposit . Inside a method, the fields of the object are just there — FBalance . private parts are for the class's own code. public parts are for everyone. The balance is private and only readable through the Balance property : nobody can set it to a million by mistake; money only moves through Deposit and Withdraw , which keep it correct. The constructor Create makes an object and sets it up; inherited Create lets the parent class here the root of all classes, TObject do its part first. Objects live until you free them TAccount.Create ... makes a new object in memory and gives back a reference to it. The variable A holds that reference, not the object itself. Pascal has no garbage collector: an object stays in memory until it is freed, so every Create needs a Free . The pattern that never forgets: try … finally runs the finally part whatever happens in the try part — even when an error chapter 9 jumps out of it. Write the try right after the Create , and the Free before anything else. To find a forgotten Free , let Free Pascal count: with these lines in pastel.toml , a debug build lists at its end every piece of memory that was not freed, and where it was made: References, not copies Because variables hold references, assigning one object variable to another does not copy the object: Compare this with records chapter 5 , where assignment copied everything. After A.Free , B points to freed memory: using it is a bug. A variable that points to nothing holds nil ; Assigned A asks whether it is not nil , and FreeAndNil A frees and sets it to nil in one step. TBox has a public field without private : fine for a tiny example; real classes keep their fields private. Properties A property looks like a field from outside, but the class decides what reading and writing it does. It can read a field directly and write through a method that checks the value: Now E.Amount := 5 cannot happen without an error. Properties can also be computed — read GetBalance calls a function — or read only, with no write at all. Inheritance A class can be built on another: it inherits all of the parent's fields, methods and properties, adds its own, and can change how inherited methods behave: class TShape makes TCircle a kind of TShape . A variable of type TShape can hold any shape. virtual methods can be replaced by child classes with override ; the object's real class decides which one runs. S.Describe on a circle runs TCircle.Describe even though S is a TShape — this is polymorphism : one loop handles every kind of shape. abstract says the parent has no code for it; every child must give one. Creating a TShape itself would be a mistake, and calling its Area an error. inherited Describe calls the parent's version from inside the child's. is asks whether an object is of a class or a child of it ; as converts the reference, with an error if it is not: S as TCircle . ClassName is the class's name, a method every object has from TObject . Destructors When a class owns other objects, it frees them in its destructor , which always looks like this: declared in the class as destructor Destroy; override; . Never call Destroy yourself — call Free , which calls Destroy and does nothing when the reference is nil . In Pocket: an entry as an object Chapter 5 kept an entry in a record. As a class, it can protect its amount never negative and answer questions about itself SignedAmount : negative for an expense . This is Pocket's TEntry , here inside a small program; ch
headings: Objects live until you free them
In Pocket: an entry as an object

title: 9. When things go wrong
text: 9. When things go wrong Files are missing, users type letters where numbers belong, networks drop. A good program expects this and handles it in one place, instead of checking for errors after every line. Object Pascal does it with exceptions . An exception stops everything — unless it is caught When something goes wrong, code raises an exception: an object that describes the problem. From that point, nothing more of the current routine runs; the exception travels up through the routines that called it, until some code catches it. If nobody does, the program stops and prints the message. try … except runs the try part; if an exception is raised inside it also deep inside a routine it calls , the except part runs. on E: EConvertError do catches only exceptions of that class and its children , and E is the exception object — E.Message its text. The exception object is freed by itself after the handler. Several kinds The first on that fits is used, so put the specific ones first and Exception — the parent of all exceptions — last. Why compute Q before the WriteLn , and not write 100 div N inside it? WriteLn writes its parts one after the other: with N = 0 it would already have written 100 / 0 = when the division fails. Do the work first, then write the result. Raising your own raise throws an exception. Make a class for the kinds of problems your code has; it can be caught apart from everything else: Create takes the message; CreateFmt builds it like Format . The third Spend never runs: the exception left the try block at the second. finally and except together finally chapter 8 cleans up whatever happens; except handles a problem. They do different jobs, and often appear together — finally inside, except outside: The finally ran first on the way out of Load , then the except that caught it. Passing it on An except block can do something and let the exception go on with a bare raise; . This is how a routine undoes its half done work: That is the start of Pocket's TEntryList.AddEntry chapter 10 . When to use them Exceptions are for the unexpected : a file that should be there is not, a value that cannot be right. They carry the problem to the place that can deal with it — often the top of the program, which tells the user. For expected cases, a result is simpler. A user typing a wrong number is normal: TryStrToInt and Pocket's TryParseMoney answer False instead of raising. Use a Try… function where a failure is part of the normal flow. Catch what you can handle. on E: Exception do around everything hides bugs. Catch the kinds you expect, where you know what to do. Never leave an except empty. An error that is swallowed silently is the hardest bug to find. In a Pastel app, an exception that no code catches in an event handler a button's OnClick does not crash the app: Pastel shows its message to the user, writes it to the console, and the app goes on. Application.OnException lets you handle them all in one place. In Pocket TEntry 's Amount refuses negative values with EArgumentException chapter 8 . The command line will catch the errors the user can fix — a wrong amount, a missing file — and show them in one line; anything else stops the program with its message, because it is a bug to fix. Here is the idea in small: Exercises 1. Read a number with ReadLn and StrToInt ; catch EConvertError and ask again until it works. 2. Make EAgeError and a procedure CheckAge Age: Integer that raises it outside 0..150. Catch it in the program. 3. What does StrToInt '99999999999' raise? Find out by catching Exception and printing E.ClassName . 4. ★ Write function SafeDivide A, B: Integer; out Q: Integer : Boolean — the Try… style — and compare a program that uses it with one that catches EDivByZero . Which reads better? Next: 10. Lists, dictionaries and generics 10 generics.md
headings: An exception stops everything — unless it is caught

title: 10. Lists, dictionaries and generics
text: 10. Lists, dictionaries and generics Arrays chapter 5 hold a row of values, but growing them by hand gets tedious, and finding a value means a loop. This chapter brings the containers every program uses: lists that grow by themselves, lists that own their objects, and dictionaries that find a value by its key. They are generic : written once, for any type. TStringList The oldest and handiest list holds strings. It is in the Classes unit: It also reads and writes text files a line each LoadFromFile , SaveToFile , can keep itself sorted Sorted := True and refuse doubles Duplicates := dupIgnore . Generic lists The unit Generics.Collections has containers for any type. You choose the type of the elements when you use one — specialize TList<Integer is a list of integers: specialize is the word {$mode objfpc} uses to make a type from a generic one; the type section gives it a name. In {$mode delphi} you write TList<Integer without it — see appendix B. Add , AddRange , Insert I, X put elements in Delete I , Remove X , Clear take them out L I , Count , First , Last read them from 0 IndexOf X , Contains X find one Sort , Reverse order them ToArray a dynamic array of them Lists of objects A TObjectList holds objects and, unless told otherwise, owns them: removing an object from the list, or freeing the list, frees the object too. No loop of Free s, no leaks: TItemList.Create False makes a list that does not own its objects: right when it only points to objects that belong to another list — a filtered view, say. Then it must not free them, and the owner must outlive it. Dictionaries A TDictionary finds a value by its key at once, however many there are: Add refuses a key that is already there an exception ; AddOrSetValue replaces. Prices 'cake' raises when the key is missing; TryGetValue answers False instead. A dictionary has no order . To list it sorted, copy its pairs ToArray or keys into a list and sort that. {$WARN 4046 OFF} : Free Pascal 3.2 warns about its own code when a TDictionary is made "Constructing a class … with abstract method" . The warning is harmless; this line switches it off for the unit. Sorting your way Sort orders numbers and strings by themselves. For anything else, give it a function that compares two elements — negative when the first goes first, positive when the second does, 0 when equal: constref passes the elements without copying them — the comparer's rule. TComparer<T .Construct turns the function into what Sort takes. Writing a generic type You can write generic types too. The type parameter is a placeholder that the user fills in: The record has methods — Free Pascal calls them advanced records , and {$modeswitch advancedrecords} under the mode line turns them on. In Pocket: the list of entries Pocket keeps its entries in a TObjectList of TEntry with methods of its own — totals, a month, the categories. Here is the whole unit, src/pocketentries.pas ; TEntry is the class from chapter 8, with an Assign that copies another entry's values: <! file: examples/pocket core/src/pocketentries.pas What to notice: TEntryList = class specialize TObjectList<TEntry — a class built on a generic one. It is an object list Add , Count , for … in , owning and adds Pocket's methods. Inside them, Self is the list. AddEntry makes the entry, and frees it again if setting a value raises chapter 9 : a list never holds a half made entry, and nothing leaks. InMonth returns a new list made with Create False : it points to the same entries without owning them. The caller frees only the list. Categories uses a sorted TStringList that ignores doubles, and returns its strings as an array. SortByDate sorts with a comparing function, newest first. And the reports — a month in short, and the total of each category — in src/pocketreports.pas : <! file: examples/pocket core/src/pocketreports.pas TotalsByCategory adds up the amounts per category in a dictionary, then copies them into an array of records and sorts it,

title: 11. Files and JSON
text: 11. Files and JSON A program forgets everything when it ends — unless it writes it down. This chapter writes and reads files, and uses JSON, the text format nearly every program and web service understands. At the end, Pocket keeps its entries between runs. Text files the easy way Pastel.Files reads and writes whole files in one call — always as UTF 8, on every system: ReadText , WriteText , AppendText a whole file as one string ReadLines , WriteLines as an array of lines ReadBytes , WriteBytes any file, as bytes JoinPath 'a', 'b', 'c.txt' a path with the system's separator / or \ EnsureDir , DeleteDir , ListFiles Dir, ' .txt' folders HomeDir , AppDir , MakeTempDir where things are FileExists , DirectoryExists SysUtils is it there? Build paths with JoinPath , never by adding '/' : the same code then works on Windows. The classic way Pascal's own text files read a line at a time — useful for files too big to read at once: WriteLn F, … and ReadLn F, … are the screen's WriteLn and ReadLn , aimed at a file. JSON JSON writes data as text that both people and programs can read: Objects in {} hold named values, arrays in hold lists; values are strings, numbers, true / false , null , or more objects and arrays. Free Pascal's fpjson unit keeps JSON as objects: TJSONObject , TJSONArray , and values — all children of TJSONData . Pastel.Json adds short helpers that read values by a path: ParseJson turns text into objects — and you free what it gives back. JStr , JInt , JFloat , JBool read a value by its path: names with dots, array elements with 0 . A missing value gives the default the third parameter instead of an error, which suits data from outside. JArray gives the elements of an array, for a for … in loop. Writing JSON JObject makes an object from names and values in one line; a TJSONArray collects objects. ToJson writes them as text, SaveJsonFile into a file: A TJSONArray owns what is added to it: freeing the array frees the objects inside. In Pocket: keeping the entries Pocket keeps its entries in a JSON file — a list of objects, one per entry: Dates are written as yyyy mm dd text: readable, sortable, and the same in every country. The kind is written as a word, not as 0 or 1 , so the file still makes sense when the enumeration changes. Saving and loading are two procedures: New here: JArray Data, '' — the empty path is the value itself: the list of entries. JFloat reads a number as a Double ; assigning it to a Currency rounds it to four decimal places — for amounts with cents, exact again. AddEntry ... .Id := 1 sets a property of the object a function returned, without a variable. KindName E.Kind :8 — in Write and WriteLn , a : and a number give the width, aligned right. A quick way to make columns. Chapter 13 turns this pair of procedures into a store : one object that knows where the entries are kept — first this JSON file, later a database — and the rest of Pocket does not need to know which. Exercises 1. Write a program that counts the lines, words and bytes of a text file given as ParamStr 1 . 2. Save a TStringList of names to a file, load it in a second run, and add a name each time. 3. Load pocket.json and print the total of each kind. Then change a number in the file by hand and run it again. 4. ★ Make LoadEntries safe against a broken file: catch the exception of LoadJsonFile , and raise one of your own EStoreError that names the file and says what was wrong. Next: 12. Testing 12 testing.md

title: 12. Testing
text: 12. Testing You changed TryParseMoney to accept a new way of writing amounts. Does 12,50 still work? And 7 ? Checking by hand after every change is slow, and one day you forget. A test is a small piece of code that checks a piece of your program and says pass or fail — and the computer runs hundreds of them in a second, every time. A test suite Tests live in the tests/ folder of a project. A test unit has a class built on TTestSuite ; every published method is one test : Run them: Pastel finds the test units in tests/ , builds them into a test program and runs it. The method names become the test names — so name them as sentences about what should be true. Asserts AssertEquals Expected, Actual for strings, whole numbers, Double with a tolerance , Boolean AssertTrue Condition , AssertFalse Condition anything else AssertContains Part, Text , AssertStartsWith Start, Text parts of text AssertNil X , AssertNotNil X references AssertRaises EClass, @Proc that a procedure raises an exception Fail Message fail here a line that must not be reached Skip Reason not here a database server that is not running Every assert takes a last parameter, a message that is shown when it fails — use it when the line alone would not say what went wrong. The expected value comes first : a failure then reads "expected 1,234.50 but got 1234.50 ". A failing test shows where: Testing exceptions Two ways: AssertRaises , or a try with Fail in it — this one also lets you look at the message: SetUp and TearDown When every test of a suite needs the same start — a list with sample entries, an empty folder — override SetUp runs before each test and TearDown after each, also when it failed : Tests must not depend on each other or on their order: each one starts clean. Choosing and watching In VS Code the Testing view lists every test with a ▶ to run it, and the failing line is marked in the editor. What to test Test the parts with rules: parsing, calculations, decisions — Pocket's money, its totals, its store. Each test checks one thing and its name says which. When you find a bug, first write a test that fails because of it, then fix the code: the bug can never come back unnoticed. A library: code for more than one program Pocket will have two programs: the command line chapter 13 and the app part 2 . Both need the same entries, money and reports. Copying the units would mean fixing every bug twice. Instead, they go into a library project that both programs use: Move the units of chapters 7–11 into pocket core/src/ , and the tests into pocket core/tests/ . Then each program names the library in its pastel.toml : Now uses PocketMoney finds the library's unit, and pastel build compiles it with the program. A fix in pocket core reaches both programs at their next build. Libraries can also come from git or from Pastel's package registry packages.md ../packages.md . The book's projects sit side by side: All of Pocket's tests are in examples/pocket core/tests/pocket test.pas ../../examples/pocket core/tests/pocket test.pas : money, the list, the reports, both stores and the bank import. Exercises 1. Make the library, move the units, and run pastel test in it. 2. Add a test for FormatMoney 0.005 . What should it give? Chapter 4 decided. 3. Write tests for TEntryList.Categories : empty list, one category, the same category twice in different case. 4. ★ Break TotalsByCategory on purpose sort smallest first and watch which test fails. Then fix it again. Next: 13. Interfaces and the command line 13 interfaces.md
headings: A library: code for more than one program

title: 13. Interfaces and the command line
text: 13. Interfaces and the command line Pocket keeps its entries in a JSON file. In part 2 the app will keep them in a database. The code that uses the entries should not care where they live — and with an interface , it does not. At the end of this chapter, part 1 is done: Pocket is a finished command line program. An interface is a promise An interface lists methods, without code. A class that implements it promises to have them: ISpeaker = interface lists what a speaker can do. By custom, interface names start with I . The GUID in brackets any unique one: uuidgen in a terminal makes one lets the program ask an object at run time whether it has the interface Supports , as . TDog = class TInterfacedObject, ISpeaker — a class, built on TInterfacedObject , that implements ISpeaker . Introduce takes any speaker. It does not know dogs or robots, and never will need to. How is that different from a parent class with a virtual method chapter 8 ? A class has only one parent, but it can implement many interfaces — a TDog could also be an IPet and an ISerializable . Interfaces describe what an object can do , not what it is . No Free: reference counting There is no Free in that program, and no leak. An object used through an interface counts how many interface variables point to it; when the count drops to zero, it frees itself. S := TRobot.Create dropped the dog's count to zero. The rule that comes with it: use such an object only through interface variables. Mixing a class variable and an interface variable for the same object leads to an object freed too early, or freed twice. Pocket's store follows the rule — the program holds an IEntryStore , never a TJsonStore . Pocket's store The store is an interface with three methods, and its first implementation keeps the entries in the JSON file of chapter 11 — the procedures of that chapter, moved into a class. src/pocketstore.pas in pocket core : <! file: examples/pocket core/src/pocketstore.pas New things in it: EStoreError is the exception for everything that can go wrong with the kept data; a program catches it to show the user one clear line. TJsonStore.Load wraps LoadJsonFile 's exception in an EStoreError that names the file. IsoToDate checks the date with TryEncodeDate instead of trusting the file. Save gives entries without an id the next free one. The comment around the file's example uses … : the JSON in it has { } , which would end a { } comment early. The app in part 2 adds a second store, TDbStore , with a database behind the same three methods. Pocket on the command line Command line programs take arguments : pocket add 12.50 Food note Lunch . Pastel.Args reads them: you describe the commands, options and flags, and it parses the command line, checks it, and writes the help: <! file: examples/pocket cli/src/main.pas How it fits together: The description : Args.Command 'add', … makes a sub command with its own Positional arguments, Option s date 2026 11 03 or d … and Flag s income . .Env 'POCKET FILE' lets an environment variable give the option; .Default ... is used when neither does. Args.Parse reads the real command line; for help , version or a mistake it prints what is needed and ends the program. One routine per command , chosen with case Args.CommandName of . Each is short because the work is in the library. Errors the user can fix — a wrong amount, a missing entry, a broken file — are exceptions EArgsError , EStoreError caught in one place at the bottom: one line on the error output and an exit code 0 is success; scripts check it . Anything else is a bug and stops the program with its message. InMonth.Free in ListCommand and ReportCommand — the leak of chapter 10, fixed. TTable from Pastel.Term lines up the columns, also with letters like ş . The project file of pocket cli names the library: Using it pocket help lists the commands, and pocket add help the options of one. pastel build release makes the program you give to others; pastel package pack

title: 14. Your first window
text: 14. Your first window Part 1 wrote programs that talk through the terminal. Most people expect a window: buttons, fields, lists. This chapter makes one, explains how a Pastel app is put together, and starts Pocket's app. A new app A window opens with a field and two buttons. Type your name and press Send . In VS Code: Pastel: New Project… → Desktop App , then F9 . The project: Every window — a form — is two files with the same name: a .pform that says what is in it and a .pas that says what it does . This is Delphi's .dfm and .pas , and the same idea as HTML and its script. The program src/main.pas is short and rarely changes: Application from Pastel.App is the app: Initialize sets it up fonts, language, theme , CreateForm makes the window from its .pform , and Run shows it and answers the mouse and keyboard until the window is closed. The first form created is the main window. The layout: a .pform file Shortened: the real file has a hint line and a Clear button too. object Name: TType … end makes a control; objects inside another become its children. The lines set properties — the published properties of the class, which you met in chapter 8. Text in single quotes, numbers plain, True / False , choices by name TextAlign = Center , sets in brackets. OnClick = SendClick connects an event to a method of the form. Layout = Free places every control where its Left and Top say, as in Delphi. Anchors = Left, Top, Right stretches the edit when the window gets wider. Chapter 15 shows the other way to lay out, which Pocket uses. The code: Home.pas Where do NameEdit and Greeting come from? From Home.g , a unit Pastel generates from the .pform at every build: THomeForm inherits from THomeFormBase chapter 8 , so every control of the .pform is a field of your form, with the right type. Rename a control in the .pform and the compiler shows every line of code that still uses the old name. The generated code never mixes with yours. An event handler is a method with the signature the event wants — for a click, procedure X Sender: TObject , where Sender is the control that was clicked. One handler can serve several controls: OnSubmit of the edit Enter pressed in it and OnClick of the button both call SendClick . Hot reload Run the app with pastel run , then change Text = 'Hello!' in Home.pform and save . The window changes at once — no restart, and what you typed stays in the field. A debug build reads the .pform from disk and watches it; a release build has it compiled in. Changes to the .pas code need a restart: stop and press F9 again, or let pastel run watch restart the app whenever a file is saved. The designer Open Home.pform in VS Code and press the designer button in the editor's title bar. It is laid out like Delphi: the Structure and Object Inspector with Properties and Events on the left, the form in the middle, the Tool Palette on the right. Drag a control from the palette onto the form, change its properties, double click an event to write its handler. F12 switches between the form and its code. Every change in the designer is an ordinary edit of the .pform text, and every edit of the text shows in the designer — use whichever is quicker. The designer also shows the form at phone, tablet and desktop sizes, dark, and in each platform's style. Pocket's app begins Make the app next to the library and the command line: and name the library in its pastel.toml , as pocket cli does: <! file: examples/pocket app/pastel.toml platforms lists where it will run: Linux and Windows, and Android from chapter 21. package.android id names the app on phones. The app has two forms: the main window, Home , and a dialog for one entry, EntryEditor . main.pas creates both: <! file: examples/pocket app/src/main.pas The next chapters build them: the layout chapter 15 , the list and the dialog 16 , the database 17 , the chart and reports 18 . Exercises 1. In the hello app, add a TCheckBox Shout and write the greeting in capitals when it is

title: 15. Layout
text: 15. Layout A window is not always the size you designed it for. People make it wider, a laptop has a small screen, a phone is narrow and tall. This chapter shows how Pastel places controls so that a form fits every size — and builds Pocket's main window. Two ways to place controls Free Layout = Free , chapter 14's hello : every control has a Left , Top , Width , Height , as in Delphi. Anchors decide which edges follow the window when it is resized. Quick to design by dragging, good for dialogs of a fixed size. Flow the default when Layout is not set : controls are placed one after another — under each other in a column, side by side in a row — and share the room there is. Nothing has to be placed by hand, and the form follows any size. This is how web pages and phone apps lay out, and how Pocket does it. Rows and columns A form is a column. Its children go down, one under the other; TRow puts its children side by side. TColumn , TRow children under each other / side by side TFlow side by side, going on to the next line when the row is full buttons, tags TCard a column with a background, a border and round corners TPanel a box with Layout = Free inside a flow layout TSpacer empty room that pushes the controls after it away Grow = 1 TScrollBox a column that scrolls when its content is taller And the properties that do the work: Grow takes the free room: in a column the height, in a row the width. 2 takes twice what 1 does Width , Height a fixed size; 0 not set is "as big as the content needs" Gap room between children Padding room inside the container's edges Align across: Stretch the default: full width in a column , Start , Center , End Justify along: Start , Center , End , SpaceBetween MinWidth , MinHeight a form the smallest the window may get MaxContentWidth the children at most this wide, in the middle: readable on a big screen Pocket's main window Here is the whole layout of Pocket's main window: <! file: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pform Read it from the top: a header row the arrows around the month, which Grow = 1 pushes to the edges , a row of three cards that share the width each Grow = 1 , the main row that takes all the height left Grow = 1 in the form with the list growing beside a chart of a fixed width, and a TFlow of buttons that wraps onto a second line when the window is narrow. Not one Left or Top : the same file fits a big monitor and a small phone. ! Pocket on a computer images/pocket.png Windows of every size A wide window has room for the chart beside the list; a phone does not. Every form knows what kind of screen it is on — its ScreenClass : scPhone , scTablet , scTV or scDesktop a computer's window narrower than 600 counts as a phone, so you can try phone layouts by making the window narrow . OnScreenClassChange runs when the form first shows, and whenever the kind changes: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas It is connected in the .pform OnScreenClassChange = ScreenChange . On a phone the chart and the notes column go, and the date and category columns share what is left; on a computer they come back. ! Pocket on a phone images/pocket phone.png For bigger differences, a form can have views : Home.phone.pform with only the values that differ on phones sizes, Visible , texts — see forms.md ../forms.md views a form for each kind of screen . Checking a layout pastel check lays out every form at its size and warns when something cannot fit — a row whose controls need more room than there is, so the last ones would be cut off — and about unknown properties. The designer outlines the same problems on the form. And pastel preview draws a form into a picture without running the app: Exercises 1. Make a form with a TMemo that fills it and a row of three buttons at the bottom, right aligned. 2. Put two TCard s side by side, the first twice as wide as the second Grow = 2 and Grow = 1 . 3. Make Pocket's window narrow while it runs and watch ScreenChange work. Then hide the Impor

title: 16. Grids and dialogs
text: 16. Grids and dialogs Pocket's window has its layout; now it needs its entries. This chapter fills the list, adds a dialog for one entry, and asks before deleting — the everyday work of a business app. The form's data A form is a class chapter 8 , so it can keep fields of its own beside its controls. Pocket's main form keeps the store, the list of all entries, and the month shown: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas FormCreate the form's OnCreate , when the form is made opens the store and loads the entries; the destructor frees what the form made, in the other order: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas The store and DatabaseUrl are chapter 17's. Note TEntryList.Create False : FShown holds the same entries as FEntries but does not own them chapter 10 — freeing it does not free them. TGrid A TGrid shows rows and columns. Its columns are declared in the .pform chapter 15 has Pocket's : The rows are added in code, one array of strings each, in the columns' order: A cell keeps its value as data : a date as 2026 11 03 , an amount with a dot. The column's Kind decides how it is shown — in the user's language 03.11.2026 and 12,50 in Turkish — and how it sorts as a date, as a number . Never put a formatted text in a Money cell; give it the value. Row the selected row 1 : none RowCount , Cells Col, Row the rows, a cell's value RowSelect , Striped , Sortable , Editable whole rows selected, every other row shaded, a click on a title sorts, cells can be typed in OnChange the selection changed OnDblClick a double click or Enter on a row Showing a month ShowMonth puts the month on screen: the totals in the cards, the entries in the grid, the expenses in the chart chapter 18 : <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas CurrToStr …, InvariantFormat writes the amount with a dot whatever the language — the data form the grid wants. Which entry is selected? The grid holds strings; the program needs the TEntry . FShown is a list of the entries in the same order as the grid's rows , so row 3 is FShown 3 : <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas EntriesChange runs when the selection changes OnChange = EntriesChange in the .pform and enables the buttons that need a selected entry. ShowMonth calls it too, with nil as the Sender — a handler is an ordinary method. The arrows move between months: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas A dialog: one entry Adding and changing an entry uses the same small form, EntryEditor : <! file: examples/pocket app/src/forms/EntryEditor.pform ! The entry dialog images/entry dialog.png New controls here: TComboBox a choice from a list: Items , ItemIndex 0 the first TCurrencyEdit an amount: Value a Currency , Valid what was typed is an amount — it reads 12,50 and 12.50 both TDatePicker a date with a calendar: Date , HasDate TEdit.Completions words offered while typing — here the categories used before Two buttons close the dialog. Cancel has ModalResult = mrCancel : a click closes it with that result, no code needed. Cancel = True makes Escape press it, Default = True makes Enter press Save . The dialog's code The dialog does not know about the store or the list. It gets an entry to show Start , checks what was typed OkClick , and gives the values back ReadInto : <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/EntryEditor.pas <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/EntryEditor.pas When something is wrong, the dialog says why and stays open , with the cursor in the field to fix. Only when all is well does it set ModalResult := mrOk — which closes it. A dialog that only does its own job can be used from anywhere: a second window, a test. That is the same rule as chapter 7's units: each part knows as little as it can. Showing it: ShowModal waits, as in Delphi — but phones cannot wait: an Android app must go back to the system while a dialog is o

title: 17. A database
text: 17. A database Chapter 11 kept Pocket's entries in a JSON file: read everything when the program starts, write everything when it changes. That is fine for a hundred entries. An app that is changed every day, by a click here and a delete there, wants a database : it writes only what changed, it cannot be left half written when the battery dies, and it finds the rows you ask for without reading the rest. SQL in one page A relational database keeps tables : rows with the same columns, like a sheet. You talk to it in SQL , a language of its own: primary key makes id the row's number, given by the database. where chooses rows, order by sorts them. Dates as YYYY MM DD text sort in the right order — the reason Pocket stores them that way. Pastel.Db Pastel.Db speaks to SQLite a database in one file, nothing to install , PostgreSQL and MySQL with the same code. A TDatabase is opened from an address: Db.Exec SQL, values create , update , delete : the number of rows changed Db.Insert SQL, values an insert : the new row's id Db.Query SQL, values the rows, as a TJSONArray of objects chapter 11 — you free it Db.QueryOne SQL, values the first row, or nil Db.QueryInt , Db.QueryValue the first column of the first row, as a number or a text Values go in as ? Never build SQL with + : If Name came from a field and someone typed x' or '1'='1 , the first line deletes every row. With ? the value is sent apart from the SQL and is only ever a value. This mistake — SQL injection — is one of the most common security holes there is; ? rules it out. Pocket's store in a database Chapter 13 made IEntryStore an interface so that the place the entries are kept can change. Here is the third store, built on a database: <! file: examples/pocket core/src/pocketdbstore.pas Points to look at: The table is made when missing create table if not exists , so a new app on a new phone starts with an empty table. A bigger app uses migrations — numbered SQL files run once each, in order database.md ../database.md migrations the tables . Load reads the rows back as JSON , with JStr , JFloat and JInt from chapter 11. Put writes one entry : an insert for a new one, which gives it its id, an update for a changed one. The app calls it after every edit, so nothing is lost if the app is closed or killed. Save uses a transaction : everything between BeginTransaction and Commit happens together or not at all. If writing the 500th entry fails, the finally frees the transaction without Commit and the table is as it was — never half old and half new. PutIn takes a TDbSession : both TDatabase and TDbTransaction are one, so the same code writes inside a transaction or outside it. Because it is an IEntryStore , pocket cli could use it with no change but one line — try exercise 1. Where the file lives The app must keep its database where it may write, and where the user's files are not: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas GetAppConfigDir is the app's own folder — ~/.config/pocket app on Linux, AppData\Local\pocket app on Windows. An Android app has a private folder of its own and starts in it, so a plain name is enough there. {$IFDEF ANDROID} compiles a part only for one platform; use it sparingly, for the few places where platforms really differ. The environment variable POCKET DB overrides the place. The app's tests use it to start with a database of their own — sqlite::memory: or a file in a temporary folder — and never touch the real one. Exercises 1. Give pocket cli a db option: with it, the command line keeps its entries in a TDbStore instead of the JSON file. 2. Write a select that gives the month's expenses by category straight from the database group by , where day like '2026 11 %' . Compare it with TotalsByCategory . 3. Try the delete with + from above on a table of your own, with the evil name. Then with ? . 4. ★ Add a column account to the table without losing the entries of people who already have the app. Hint: alter table , and how woul

title: 18. Charts and reports
text: 18. Charts and reports Numbers in a list answer "how much?"; a picture answers "where did it go?" at a glance. And sooner or later someone wants it on paper: the month for the tax adviser, an Excel file for the bank. This chapter adds Pocket's chart and its two exports. TChart TChart draws bars, lines, pies and donuts. Pocket's is declared in the .pform chapter 15 : and filled in code: the labels , then one or more series of numbers, one number per label. A pie or a donut shows the first series, one slice per label, and a donut writes the total in its middle. Bars and lines show every series side by side — this year against last year: The value under the mouse or the finger is shown by the chart itself; OnItemClick tells which bar or slice was clicked. ShowValues writes the numbers on it, Stacked puts the bars on top of each other. In ShowMonth chapter 16 the chart gets the month's expenses by category, from TotalsByCategory of chapter 10: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas TotalsByCategory gives records; the chart wants two arrays. The loop grows each by one — fine for a dozen categories for thousands, set the length once with SetLength Labels, Count . A month with no expenses gets no series: the chart stays empty. A PDF report Pastel.Report makes documents that flow over pages: a title, text, tables, totals. Everything is written from top to bottom; a full page starts a new one, and a table repeats its heads there. Table takes the heads, the widths in millimetres 0 : what is left and how each column is aligned: L , R , C . The cells are text — the report writes what you give it, so you format the numbers with Money , below . The letters come from a TrueType font of the system, and only the letters used go into the file: a page is about 30 KB, and ş , ğ , İ , € print right everywhere. An Excel file Pastel.Sheets writes .xlsx files. Unlike the report, it takes values : numbers, dates and True / False go into Excel as such, so the person who opens the file can sum, sort and chart them. Row takes an array of const chapter 10's open arrays : each value keeps its type. A TDateTime is a Double , so EncodeDate goes in as a number Excel shows as a date. ReadSpreadsheet and ReadCsv read such files back — chapter 20 uses them for the bank import. Pocket's exports The PDF and Excel buttons both call ExportMonth with the file's extension. On a computer it asks where to save; on a phone, where there is no such dialog, the file goes into the app's temporary folder: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas SaveFileDialog does not wait chapter 16 : it calls ExportTo with the name chosen. ExportTo then writes one of the two files: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas Look at the difference between the two branches. The report gets texts , formatted for a person to read: FormatDateShort E.Date , Money E.SignedAmount . The sheet gets values : E.Date , Double E.SignedAmount — Excel formats them in the reader's own language. At the end the file is opened: OpenDocument from Pastel.Print starts the system's program for it — a PDF viewer, Excel or LibreOffice. On a phone, ShareFile opens the share menu mail, Drive, a messenger , the way phone apps hand files on. PrintFile FileName would send the PDF straight to the printer. Month is a list that InMonth made for this method, so the method frees it — in a finally , because a full disk makes SaveToFile raise an exception. Exercises 1. Make the chart a bar chart of the last six months' expenses one label per month, one series . 2. Add a second table to the report: the income by category. 3. Add a column Kind to the Excel file, with Expense or Income , and a second sheet with the totals by category AddSheet . 4. ★ Open the PDF in a browser on a web server: give pocket cli a serve command that answers /report/2026/11 with R.ToBytes web.md ../web.md .
