title: 19. Look and languages
text: 19. Look and languages Pocket works. Now it should feel at home: in the colors you choose, in the look of each platform, light or dark as the user likes, and in the user's language — with numbers and dates written the way they write them. The theme: assets/theme.toml <! file: examples/pocket app/assets/theme.toml accent is the color of default buttons, selections, focus and the chart's first slice; dark gives the colors for the dark theme. Other names: background , surface cards, lists , text , text muted , border , danger , radius the corners , font size — the full list is in styles.md ../styles.md your colors over a style . Pick an accent that has enough contrast with white text in the light theme and with the dark background in the dark one, and look at both before you decide below . Light and dark The main form says Appearance = System chapter 15 : light or dark as the computer or phone is set, and it follows when the user switches while the app runs. Light or Dark fixes one. Try it: PASTEL THEME=dark pastel run . ! Pocket, dark images/pocket dark.png Colors you write yourself — like the dialog's red error text, Color = ' DC2626' — stay the same in both themes. Keep them few, and choose ones that read on both backgrounds. A style for each platform style = "auto" gives each platform its own look: Fluent on Windows Windows 11's controls , Material on Android, Pastel 's own elsewhere. The style sets the sizes and shapes — round buttons on Android, a line under the edits on Windows — and the order of a dialog's buttons. The same .pform gets each look with no change. style = "fluent" would give every platform the Windows look, and a style file of your own in assets/styles/ changes any part of one styles.md ../styles.md . Languages Texts in code: Every text a user reads goes through from Pastel.Lang : it gives the translation in the current language, or the text itself when there is none. Translate the whole sentence with its placeholders , never pieces glued together: '%d entries imported' , not IntToStr N + ' entries imported' . Other languages put the number elsewhere, and translators need the whole sentence to see what it means. The texts of the .pform files — Text , Title , Hint , Placeholder , Items — are translated without . The language files pastel lang finds the texts in the .pform files and in every '...' call. Pocket's Turkish file starts: The app uses the computer's language when there is a file for it. To try another: PASTEL LANG=tr pastel run . In code, UseLanguage 'tr' switches. Numbers, dates and months A language is more than words. Turkish writes 1.234,50 for 1,234.50 , 03.11.2026 for 11/3/2026 , and Kasım for November. Pastel.Lang does these: UseLanguage sets the formats even when there is no translation file — de has its numbers and dates here, and its month names once a de.json gives them November is the same word in German anyway . This is why Pocket's app writes money with its own little function: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas and not with FormatMoney of chapter 7, which always writes 1,234.50 . FormatMoney stays right for the command line and the files — data should look the same everywhere; only what people read changes with the language. The grid chapter 16 does the same on its own: its Money and Date columns get the values and show them in the user's language. Reading what people type follows the language too: TCurrencyEdit reads 12,50 in Turkish, and TryParseNumber does the same in code. Exercises 1. Change the accent to a color of your own, for the light and the dark theme. Look at both with pastel preview and its dark . 2. Run Pocket with PASTEL STYLE=material and PASTEL LANG=tr together, and with the dark theme. 3. Add a language of your own with pastel lang add , and translate five texts. What does the app show for the rest? 4. ★ Find a text in Home.pas that would not translate well, and fix it. Next: 20. Work in the background 20 background.md

title: 20. Work in the background
text: 20. Work in the background Most banks give a month of a bank account as a CSV file. Pocket can read one and add its rows as entries. A month is quick; ten years of a business account is not, and a file on a network drive may take seconds just to open. While the code reads, the window cannot redraw or answer a click — it freezes , and the system offers to kill it. The cure is to do slow work on another thread , and leave the main thread free for the window. The bank import First the work itself, in pocket core — plain code with no window in it, so the command line and the tests can use it too: <! file: examples/pocket core/src/pocketimport.pas It uses what part 1 taught: ReadCsv from Pastel.Sheets gives the rows as arrays of strings; the columns are found by their names in the first row, so the order does not matter; and every bad line raises an EImportError that says which line and why chapter 9 . A file like this one is read: <! file: examples/pocket app/tests/bank.csv Threads A program starts with one thread, the main one. A TThread runs its Execute method next to it, at the same time: Two halves, summed at the same time on two cores. cthreads gives Linux and macOS programs their threads; it comes first in uses . pastel build adds it to every project for you — it matters when you compile with plain fpc . The rules Threads share the program's memory, and that is what makes them hard. Two threads that change the same list at the same moment break it — not every time, only sometimes, which is worse. So: 1. A thread works on its own data. Give it what it needs before it starts; let it leave its results where only it writes. 2. Controls belong to the main thread. Never change a label, a grid or a form from another thread. 3. The main thread takes the results when the thread has finished. Threads that must share something use a lock TCriticalSection or a queue TMessageQueue from Pastel.Workers ; an app rarely needs either. RunInBackground Pastel.Workers makes the rules easy in an app. RunInBackground @Work, @Done, Data : runs Work on a thread of its own, then Done on the main thread , where controls may be changed, and gives both the same Data object, which carries what the work needs and what it found. An exception in Work does not end the program: its message is in the task's Error , for Done to show. Pocket's Import button chooses a file, then hands it to the background: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas The job object carries the file's name in and the entries out: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas The work touches nothing but the job — not FEntries , not a control: <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas Done runs on the main thread, so it may do everything else: put the entries in the list and the database, show the month, tell the user. <! part of: examples/pocket app/src/forms/Home.pas Who owns what, once more chapter 10 : the job's list owns the entries it read. They move into FEntries , so the job must stop owning them before it is freed — OwnsObjects := False — or freeing the job would free entries that FEntries still holds. And Done frees the job: the task leaves its Data to Done . Meanwhile the Import button is disabled, so a second click cannot start a second import of the same file; it comes back in Done , whether the import worked or not. Downloading The same pattern fits everything slow: a big query, a report of a thousand pages, and above all the network. A download of exchange rates with Pastel.Http would look like this: The network can be slow, or not there at all. Never ask it from the main thread — and plan for the answer that does not come. Exercises 1. Run the import with a file of 100,000 lines write it with a small program and WriteCsv . Watch the window stay alive. Then call ImportCsv directly in ImportChosen and compare. 2. Give pocket cli an

title: 21. Phones
text: 21. Phones Pocket is most useful in a pocket: the coffee is written down when it is paid, not in the evening. This chapter puts the same app — the same .pform files, the same code — on Android phones. Setting up, once Android apps are built on Linux. Install the tools and let Pastel set up the compilers: With Android Studio installed, its SDK is used as well. pastel doctor then shows the kinds of phone it can build for; android.md ../android.md setting it up once has the details. Target For android arm64 most phones since about 2016 android arm older phones, TV boxes android x86 64 the emulator and Waydroid on a PC Running it Pocket's pastel.toml chapter 14 already lists android in its platforms. Connect a phone with USB debugging on Settings → About phone , tap Build number seven times, then Developer options → USB debugging , and: Pastel asks the phone which processor it has, builds for it, packs and installs a debug .apk , starts it and shows its log until Ctrl+C. Hot reload works here too: save a .pform and the phone changes. No phone at hand? Waydroid runs Android in a window on Linux; connect adb to it adb connect with the address waydroid status shows and pastel run target android finds it like a phone. Android Studio's emulator works the same way. In VS Code, choose android in the status bar's platform box; then F9 does all of the above. What changes on a phone — and what does not Pocket needs few changes, because part 2 kept to a few rules: The layout flows chapter 15 . The form fills the screen whatever its size, and ScreenChange hides the chart and the notes column when the screen is a phone's. Dialogs do not wait chapter 16 . ShowModal @EntryDone and Ask …, @DeleteAnswered work on a phone as on a computer. Slow work is in the background chapter 20 . Android kills an app that does not answer for five seconds. Texts and numbers follow the phone's language chapter 19 , and Appearance = System its dark mode. The style is Material on Android style = "auto" : round buttons, outlined fields, and the dialogs' buttons in Android's order. ! Pocket on a phone images/pocket phone.png Taps are clicks, holding a finger is a right click, lists scroll with a swipe. The on screen keyboard comes up for an edit, and the kind it shows follows the control: TCurrencyEdit brings the number keys with a decimal point. The Back button closes the dialog on top, and on the main form the app. Where the files go Two places in Pocket know they may be on a phone. The database chapter 17 : an Android app starts in a private folder of its own, which stays when the app is updated: And the exports chapter 18 . A phone has no Save as dialog where a user picks a folder; phone apps hand files to other apps instead — mail, Drive, a messenger — through the share menu: IsMobile from Pastel.Device is true on phones and tablets. Prefer it to {$IFDEF ANDROID} : it is decided while the app runs, so the same code is right on whatever phone platform comes next. Pastel.Device has more of what phones offer: the camera and photos, the location, notifications, vibration, the contacts and calendar, sharing into the app — see device.md ../device.md . When the phone stops the app An app that is not on the screen can be stopped by Android to free memory. When the user comes back, it starts again, and Pastel puts back what the controls showed — the text of edits, the selected row, the scroll position. What is not in a control, the form keeps itself in OnSaveState : and reads back in OnCreate . Pocket's data is in the database after every change FStore.Put , so nothing is lost — which is the reason it writes at once and not when the app closes: on a phone an app is often never "closed". When it crashes shows the app's lines of the phone's log, and where a crash in the Pascal code happened file and line, from the debug build . In VS Code: Pastel: Android Log . An .apk to share makes dist/pocket app 1.0.0.apk with every kind of processor in it. Copy it

title: 22. Shipping
text: 22. Shipping Pocket runs on your computer. This last chapter gets it onto other people's: a release build, a package for each platform, a key for Android, and a way to update. Before a release A UI script drives the app like a user — clicks, typing, what the window shows — with no screen, so it runs on a build server too: POCKET DB , chapter 17: the test never touches your real entries. Pocket's is examples/pocket app/tests/ui.txt ../../examples/pocket app/tests/ui.txt ; forms.md ../forms.md testing a form without a window has the commands it may use. Then raise the version in pastel.toml — 1.0.0 to 1.0.1 for fixes, 1.1.0 for something new, 2.0.0 when old data or habits no longer fit. The program can show it: the AppVersion constant of the generated unit AppInfo is always the version of pastel.toml . Release builds A release build is optimized, smaller, and has no debugger information and no hot reload: its forms are compiled into it. It is what every pastel package below builds and packs. A package for each platform pastel package a .tar.gz Linux or .zip Windows with the program and its files pastel package deb a Debian/Ubuntu/Mint package, with a menu entry and the icon pastel package appimage one file that runs on most Linux systems pastel package installer target windows a Windows installer setup.exe , needs makensis , with a Start menu entry and an uninstaller pastel package apk an Android app for every kind of processor, to install by hand pastel package aab the bundle Google Play wants All of them can be made on Linux: the Windows program is built there too target windows . pastel package all makes one for every platform of pastel.toml . Everything lands in dist/ , each file with a .sha256 next to it — a fingerprint, for anyone who wants to check that the file is the one you made. The name under the icon is project title Pocket , the icon assets/icon.png , in every size each platform needs. Android: the key Android knows an app by the key it was signed with. A debug key is made for you; for a release, make your own, once : Every update must be signed with the same key. Keep a copy of the file and its password away from the computer. Lose them, and the app cannot be updated: it would be a new app, and every user would have to start again. keys/ is in .gitignore , so the key never lands in a public repository. Upload the .aab in Google Play's console. What Play asks of new apps — made for the newest Android, 16 KB memory pages, the icon in the phone's shape — Pastel does by itself android.md ../android.md google play . Updating itself An app from Google Play is updated by Play. One you hand out yourself can look for a new version: pastel update manifest https://example.com/pocket/ "What is new" writes dist/update.json from the packages in dist/ ; put it and them at that address. The installer, the AppImage and the .apk each know how to replace themselves system.md ../system.md updating itself pastelupdater . What you built Pocket is three projects, and every part of the book is in them: The code you read in these chapters is the code of those folders — the book is checked against it on every change of Pastel, so it cannot drift. Where next The manual : docs/ ../README.md has a page for every part of Pastel; this book left out much more than it showed — a web server and API web.md ../web.md , sign in auth.md ../auth.md , sync that works offline sync.md ../sync.md , services services.md ../services.md . The examples : examples/ ../../examples has an app for a hair salon with invoices and its server, a notepad, a contacts app, a weather app, a duplicate file finder and an API for notes. Read them like this book: start at main.pas , then the forms. Delphi and Lazarus code : Appendix B appendix b from delphi.md shows what is the same and what is not. Free Pascal itself : its reference guide freepascal.org/docs is the final word on the language. And write a program of your own — the one you need. That is how e

title: Appendix B. Coming from Delphi or Lazarus
text: Appendix B. Coming from Delphi or Lazarus Most of what you know carries over: the language is the same Object Pascal, a form is still a layout file and a unit, events are still methods with a Sender . This appendix lists what is different, so you can skip the chapters you do not need. The language: {$mode objfpc} and {$mode delphi} Free Pascal speaks several dialects. This book uses {$mode objfpc} ; {$mode delphi} is closer to what Delphi accepts. A project chooses in pastel.toml : and a unit can say it in its first lines. Units of both modes work together in one program. {$mode objfpc} {$mode delphi} and Delphi Generic types generic TBox<T = class / specialize TList<Integer TBox<T = class / TList<Integer An event handler Button.OnClick := @SaveClick; Button.OnClick := SaveClick; Result always there always there string with {$H+} : a long string, UTF 8 {$H+} is on Several routines of one name overload optional overload needed Strings Delphi's string is UTF 16 UnicodeString ; Free Pascal's, with {$H+} , is UTF 8 AnsiString with the UTF 8 code page . For most code this does not matter. Where it does: Length 'ş' is 2 bytes, not letters , and S I is a byte. Chapter 6 shows the helpers for letters Pastel.Text . Code that reads files is simpler: files are UTF 8 too. What Free Pascal has and Delphi has not or the other way Free Pascal only: generic / specialize , operators overloaded outside a type operator + A, B: TMoney : TMoney; , {$modeswitch ...} for single features advancedrecords for methods in records , for..in over an enumeration type. Delphi only not in Free Pascal 3.2 : inline variables var X := 5; inside a block and anonymous methods — use a method of the form instead; attributes are limited. Round rounds a half to the even number in both; Pastel's money code adds 0.5 and truncates chapter 4 . Forms: .dfm and .pform A .pform is a .dfm in text form, with a few names changed: Delphi VCL / FMX Pastel Caption of a form Title Caption of a button, label, check box Text Align = alTop / alClient Dock = Top / Fill in a Layout = Free parent Anchors = akLeft, akTop, akRight Anchors = Left, Top, Right Font.Size , Font.Style = fsBold FontSize , Bold = True TPageControl + TTabSheet TTabControl + TTabSheet Caption stays TStringGrid , TDBGrid TGrid with TGridColumn children TMainMenu , TPopupMenu , TActionList TMenuBar , TPopupMenu , TAction TDateTimePicker , TSpinEdit , TTrackBar TDatePicker , TNumberEdit , TSlider TPanel , TGroupBox , TTimer , TImage the same names What is new: Flow layout chapter 15 : TRow , TColumn , Grow , Gap . Delphi has TFlowPanel and TGridPanel ; here it is the normal way, and what makes a form fit a phone. The generated unit : the controls are declared in Home.g.pas , made from the .pform at every build, and your form inherits from it chapter 14 . Your .pas holds only your code. Hot reload : a saved .pform changes the running app. One look everywhere : Pastel draws its controls itself — no native widgets — and style = "auto" gives each platform its look chapter 19 , like FireMonkey's styles. pastel check tells you about properties a control does not have, so a Caption left on a button is found at once. Dialogs that do not wait ShowModal , ShowMessage , MessageDlg and the file dialogs wait, as in the VCL. Each also has a form that returns at once and calls a method with the result chapter 16 — what FireMonkey asks for on Android ShowModal procedure ModalResult: TModalResult ... . Use that form in code that should run on phones: Units: where things are Delphi Pastel Vcl.Forms , Vcl.Controls , FMX.Forms Pastel.App the Application , Pastel.UI forms and controls Vcl.Dialogs Pastel.Dialogs FireDAC , dbExpress , TDataSet Pastel.Db : rows come back as JSON chapter 17 ; TGrid.LoadJson shows them System.JSON fpjson and Pastel.Json chapter 11 System.Net.HttpClient Pastel.Http System.Threading TTask TThread as in Delphi, RunInBackground chapter 20 FastReport , QuickReport Pastel.Report chapter 18 DUnitX Pastel.Tes

title: Guide: writing a command-line tool
text: Guide: writing a command line tool This guide builds a real tool step by step: dupfinder , which finds files with the same content. The finished program is in examples/dupfinder ; a second example, examples/weather , shows a tool that calls a web API. Both are built and tested with every change to Pastel, so the code here works. 1. Start Decide what the tool should look like from the outside first. For dupfinder: 2. Keep the work out of main.pas main.pas deals with the command line and the screen. The actual work goes in a unit under src/ Pastel finds every folder below it : here src/services/duplicates.pas . A unit that does not write to the screen or read arguments is easy to test and to reuse. The idea: files of different size cannot be equal, so only files that share their size with another are read, and those are compared by MD5 checksum Free Pascal's md5 unit . 3. Test it Write the tests next to the code, in tests/duplicates test.pas . The test creates its own files in a temporary folder: Keep pastel test watch running in a terminal while you work: every save runs the tests again. MakeTempDir , WriteText , ListFiles and DeleteDir come from Pastel.Files system.md system.md . 4. Arguments Args.Parse takes care of help , version , missing folders and typing mistakes min sise → did you mean min size? , with exit code 2. All the details are in console.md console.md . 5. Check the input, say what is wrong Some mistakes only the program can see. Say them in a sentence, on standard error, and end with exit code 2 wrong use or 1 it did not work : 6. Progress for people, plain output for scripts Reading thousands of files takes a while. A progress bar helps a person at a terminal, but would only clutter a file or another program's input: 7. Output: for reading, and for other programs For people: short, with the important part in bold, and a summary. For other programs: json . It costs a few lines and makes the tool usable in scripts dupfinder json ~/Pictures jq ... : Colors and symbols switch themselves off when the output is not a terminal, and with NO COLOR or no color . 8. Settings and the web: the weather example examples/weather shows the rest of what most tools need. Settings that a user sets once, instead of typing them every time: The command line wins over the settings file, the file over the default. Calling a web API with Pastel.Http : HTTPS with certificate checks, proxies and clear error messages are taken care of. Testing without a network: the unit Forecast only builds addresses and reads answers; it never connects. The tests feed it answers saved from the real service, so they run anywhere, fast, and always give the same result: 9. Release dist/ then holds dupfinder 1.0.0 linux.tar.gz , dupfinder 1.0.0 windows.zip and so on, each with a .sha256 file. What goes into the packages besides the program is set in pastel.toml : Checklist for a good tool help explains every option, with an example version comes from pastel.toml mistakes are explained in a sentence, on standard error exit code 0 when it worked, 1 when it did not, 2 for wrong use no colors or progress bars when the output is not a terminal json or another plain format for scripts the work is in units with tests; main.pas only connects them

title: Guide: a REST API with a database
text: Guide: a REST API with a database From an empty folder to an API running on a server: tasks with a title, a priority and a done flag. About half an hour. 1. The project The parts: src/main.pas the service: opens the database, runs the migrations, adds the routes src/models/tasks.pas the model: every SQL statement about tasks src/controllers/taskscontroller.pas the controller: routes, checks, JSON answers database/migrations/ the tables tests/tasks test.pas tests of the model and the API config.toml settings while developing SQLite in data/app.db In VS Code the Pastel panel lists the routes, the jobs and the migrations; above every route is ▶ Send , which sends a request to the running API and shows the answer. 2. A new column: a migration database/migrations/002 add priority.sql : The next pastel run applies it or pastel migrate now; pastel migrate status shows what ran . Never change a migration that ran somewhere; add a new one. 3. The model In src/models/tasks.pas , select the new column everywhere and add it to Add : Values always go in as ? , never pasted into the SQL. More: database.md database.md . 4. The controller Check the input with Req.Validate ; every problem goes back at once as 422: A new route, in Routes : Errors: raise EWebError.Create 404, 'no task with this id' ; anything unexpected becomes 500 and goes to the log. More: web.md web.md . 5. Tests The tests get a fresh SQLite database each, with the migrations applied. Add one for the priority: pastel test watch runs them on every save. 6. Who may call it In config.toml : Now /api/... needs X API Key: <key Send Request in VS Code adds it from config.toml . For users who log in, use JWT instead: web.md web.md who is calling api keys and tokens . The example key CHANGE ME ... is refused, so a server never runs with it. 7. Work in the background Sending a mail when a task is done should not slow the answer down: services.md services.md background work pastelworkers . 8. PostgreSQL Nothing else changes: the same migrations and SQL run on SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL/MariaDB. Add libpq5 to package.deb depends . 9. On a server Or pastel package docker . HTTPS with Caddy or nginx in front: deploy.md deploy.md .

title: Guide: building a desktop app
text: Guide: building a desktop app This guide builds a small address book step by step: a window with a list and a form, menus and shortcuts, dialogs, a second window, and data in SQLite. The finished app is in examples/contacts ../examples/contacts ; examples/notepad ../examples/notepad is a text editor built the same way. The basics of .pform files, layout and the designer are in Forms and controls forms.md . This guide puts them together. 1. Create the project src/main.pas creates the forms and runs the app; src/forms/Home.pform is the main window and Home.pas its code. Keep pastel run going: when you save the .pform file the window updates by itself. 2. Lay out the window A row with two columns: a search box and a list on the left, the details on the right. In VS Code, the designer shows the window as you type; Size shows it at other window sizes and Dark in the dark theme. 3. Menus, shortcuts and actions A TAction is one command with a caption, a shortcut and an Enabled state. Menu items and buttons that use it show the same caption and are disabled together: and a button with Action = NewAction . The menu bar goes first in the form. TPopupMenu is a right click menu: give it items and set PopupMenu = EditMenu on a control. Shortcuts work anywhere in the window: Ctrl+N runs NewExecute . On macOS Ctrl means Cmd . 4. Event handlers Declare the handlers in the form class; the designer's → button next to an event creates them for you. 5. Dialogs All dialogs wait for the answer and return it. They are in Pastel.Dialogs , which new forms already have in their uses ; in an older form add it yourself. When a routine is missing from the uses , pastel build says where it is: The same works for the everyday routines Delphi programs use: IntToStr , Format , FormatDateTime SysUtils , TStringList Classes , Min , Max Math , IncDay DateUtils . MessageDlg with Danger = True makes the first button red. The save dialog asks before replacing a file. Messages and questions are drawn by Pastel inside the window. The file dialogs are the system's own Windows; on Linux zenity or kdialog when installed and Pastel's drawn ones otherwise; test scripts always get Pastel's, so they can be scripted step 9 . UseNativeDialogs := False always uses Pastel's. 6. A second window creates Settings.pform / Settings.pas with OK and Cancel buttons and adds the form to main.pas . Show it as a dialog: A button with ModalResult = mrOk closes the dialog with that result; Default = True is pressed by Enter, Cancel = True by Escape. Before closing, OnCloseQuery can say no for example when a field is empty . ShowModal waits until the dialog is closed. Its second form does not wait: it returns at once and calls a method of yours with the result — the better way in apps for phones, where nothing should wait inside an event Delphi's ShowModal procedure ... on Android : The messages and questions have the same two forms: ShowMessage 'Saved.' / ShowMessage 'Saved.', @Done , Ask 'Delete?' / Ask 'Delete?', @DeleteAnswered the method gets mrYes or mrNo , MessageDlg ..., @Done , InputQuery Title, Prompt, Value, @NameTyped gets Ok and the text , and the file dialogs OpenFileDialog FileName, Filter, Title, @FileChosen , TOpenDialog.Execute @FileChosen ; they get Ok and the file . 7. Keeping the data Put the data code in its own unit under src/services/ , not in the form: then it can be tested without a window. contactstore.pas ../examples/contacts/src/services/contactstore.pas keeps the contacts in SQLite with Pastel.Db : GetAppConfigDir False is the right place for an app's files: ~/.config/contacts on Linux, AppData\Local\contacts on Windows. See Databases database.md for transactions and migrations, and Testing testing.md for pastel test . Tables and data binding A TListView shows rows with columns; a TGrid can also edit cells. Columns take their value from the field named in Field : A click on a column title sorts Sortable = False turns it off , and only the visible rows are dr

title: Guide: a business system — desktop app and server
text: Guide: a business system — desktop app and server Many small businesses need the same thing: a program at the reception that works even when the internet does not, and a server that keeps everything together, for a second computer, a web page or a phone app. This guide shows how the salon example is built, so you can build your own a clinic, a repair shop, a warehouse the same way. ! The salon app in Turkish images/salon.png The example has three projects: Project Kind What it is examples/salon core ../examples/salon core lib The data, its checks and the synchronization — shared examples/salon desk ../examples/salon desk app The desktop app: SQLite on the computer, Sync button examples/salon api ../examples/salon api service The server: PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite; POST /api/sync 1. Put the data in a library The checks "a customer needs a name", "an e mail has an @" and the SQL must be the same on the desktop and on the server. So they go into a library, used by both: The store works on any database Pastel.Db knows; the desktop gives it a SQLite file, the server what its settings say: Records are JSON objects what Pastel.Db returns , so they go straight into lists, data bindings and HTTP answers: Two rules make synchronization possible later — follow them from the first day: Ids are made where the record is made NewId : 16 random characters , not by the database autoincrement . Two computers that both add a customer offline never get the same id. Nothing is really deleted. Delete sets deleted = 1 , so the deletion can travel to the other computers like any change. Money is kept in cents price cents , an Int64 : 0.10 + 0.20 is exactly 0.30 , and VAT is rounded once, on purpose VatOf . 2. Work offline, remember what changed Every Save writes updated at the time, UTC, sortable as text: 2026 11 01T09:30:00.123000Z and dirty = 1 : "changed here, not sent yet". The desktop works on its own file all day; the network is only needed for the Sync button. 3. Synchronize One request does everything: All of it is Pastel.Sync sync.md : the store TSyncStore , which TSalonStore uses for its tables , the client SyncWithServer and the server's route AddSyncRoute . For a system of your own, start from it. The desktop side SalonSync ../examples/salon core/src/salonsync.pas : The server side saloncontroller.pas ../examples/salon api/src/controllers/saloncontroller.pas — the same store, one line: When the same record was changed on two computers, the newer change wins updated at : Apply stores a record only when it is newer than the one there. That makes the sync safe to repeat — sending the same records twice changes nothing — and a failed sync loses nothing: the records stay dirty and go next time. "Since" uses the server's clock synced at , not the computers': their clocks may be wrong by minutes, the server's is one clock for all. The tests sync two "desktops" and a "server" three SQLite files by hand, without HTTP: tests/store test.pas ../examples/salon core/tests/store test.pas — the newer change wins, deletions travel, syncing twice changes nothing. tests/sync api test.pas ../examples/salon api/tests/sync api test.pas does it over real HTTP. 4. The desktop app Three pages in a TTabControl ; each page is a list TListView with a form next to it: The day is a TDatePicker with ‹ › and Today buttons; changing it reloads the list OnChange . Customers use a TDataBinding : CustomerData.Load Row fills the form, CustomerData.ToJson is the record to save. The settings server address, API key, VAT are a second form shown with ShowModal , remembered by a TFormMemory . Every text is in '...' or the .pform ; pastel lang add tr made assets/lang/tr.json . 5. The server A pastel new api project with the template's tasks replaced by one controller. In production: Put it behind HTTPS deploy.md deploy.md ; the read only routes /api/customers , /api/appointments?date= , /api/invoices are there for a web page or a phone app. 6. Invoices on paper,

title: Forms and controls
text: Forms and controls A Pastel window is a form . Each form has two files in src/forms/ : File What it contains Home.pform The layout: which controls exist and their properties Home.pas The code: event handlers and logic When you build, Pastel generates a third unit, Home.g , with a THomeFormBase class that has a field for every control in the .pform file. Your form class inherits from it, so you can use NameEdit.Text directly. You never edit the generated file; it lives in build/ . The .pform format object Name: TType ... end creates a control. Objects inside another object become its children. Text values use single quotes: 'It''s fine' two quotes for one . Numbers: Width = 200 , Gap = 2 . True / False for yes/no properties. Choices can be written short: Align = Center is the same as Align = aiCenter . Sets are in brackets: Anchors = Left, Top, Right . Colors are text: Color = ' 4F46E5' also RGB and AARRGGBB . Events name a method of your form class: OnClick = SendClick . The method must be declared in the class: procedure SendClick Sender: TObject ; Comments: // to the end of the line and { like this } . The window Window settings are properties of the form: Property Default Title 'Pastel' Window title Width , Height 480 × 360 Size when the window opens MinWidth , MinHeight 200 × 120 Smallest size the user can resize to Resizable True False : fixed size, no maximize WindowState Normal Maximized , Minimized or FullScreen when the window opens AlwaysOnTop False Keep the window above other windows From code: Maximize , Minimize , Restore , Close , or set WindowState and Resizable while the app runs. WindowState also tells you what the user did for example wsMaximized after they maximized the window . Window events: OnClose runs when the window really closes, OnResize after the size changed. The minimize, maximize and close buttons in the title bar are drawn by the operating system, so they always match the platform. The app's icon assets/icon.png is the app's icon everywhere: pastel new app puts Pastel's there, to be replaced by a square PNG of your own 512 × 512 is best . In VS Code: Pastel: Set App Icon… also in the Pastel side bar, and on a .png in the Explorer's right click menu . Where How the icon gets there The window and the taskbar Linux, Windows the program sets it when it opens its window The .exe in Explorer Windows built into the .exe by pastel build target windows The menu and the dock Linux the .desktop file of pastel package deb and of the AppImage; installed, the dock shows it a program run straight from build/ has no menu entry, so GNOME's dock may show a plain icon for it The Windows installer pastel package installer The phone's home screen pastel package apk , in Android's five sizes android.md android.md Designing in VS Code ! The form designer: Structure, Object Inspector, the form with a selected edit and its grips, the Tool Palette images/designer.png With the Pastel extension, open a .pform file and press the designer button in the editor title. It is laid out like Delphi's IDE: Structure and the Object Inspector with Properties and Events tabs and a search box on the left, the form in a window frame in the middle, the Tool Palette grouped, with a search box on the right; timers, actions and other non visual components sit in a tray under the form. A form made before Pastel 1.4 stacks its controls Layout = Flow , so they move only up and down; the designer then shows Place freely , which turns it into Layout = Free with every control kept where it is now. The ⇱ Place freely button under a selected row, column or card does the same for that container. Hovering over a control in the palette shows where it works Windows ✓ Linux ✓, and whether it will be on Android ; the inspector shows the same under the control's class. A menu bar, a splitter and a status bar are desktop only. In a form or panel with Layout = Free : drop a control from the palette where it should be; it snaps to an 8 pixel grid

title: Styles: Fluent, Material and your own
text: Styles: Fluent, Material and your own Pastel draws every control itself, so a form looks the same everywhere. A style changes how the controls look: their sizes, corners, borders, focus and colors. Like Delphi's FireMonkey styles, each platform has its own, and you can write your own in a style file Delphi's TStyleBook . Style Looks like Buttons Edits pastel Pastel's own look, the same everywhere 8 px corners a box, a soft ring when focused fluent Windows 11 32 px high, small corners, a border on secondary buttons a line at the bottom, the accent when focused material Android Material 3 40 px high, round ends; flat buttons are text buttons in the accent an outline, thicker when focused auto the platform it runs on: Fluent on Windows, Material on Android, Pastel elsewhere The style also sets checkboxes, radio buttons, switches, sliders, progress bars, the corners of lists, popups and dialogs, and the order of a dialog's buttons OK Cancel on Windows . ! The same form in the Pastel, Fluent and Material styles images/styles.png Choosing the style In assets/theme.toml : New apps pastel new app have this line. Without it, an app uses pastel , as before 2.1. style = "fluent" gives every platform the Windows look. The light and dark themes stay: every style has both, and Appearance on the main form chooses one as before. From code, while the app runs the form is laid out and drawn again : To try one without changing the files: PASTEL STYLE=fluent pastel run . The designer in VS Code has a style box in its top bar, and pastel preview takes style : Your colors over a style The colors of assets/theme.toml are put over the style's colors, in every style: Names: accent , on accent , background , surface , text , text muted , placeholder , secondary , border , outline the border of edits in Fluent and Material , danger , disabled , tooltip back , tooltip text , radius , font size . Hover and pressed shades follow the color. A style file A style of your own is a TOML file in assets/styles/ ; its file name is its name. It starts from a base style and changes what it says: Use it in assets/theme.toml with style = "company" . The designer and pastel preview find the project's style files too. Section Values top base , radius colors , colors.dark the theme's colors, as in theme.toml button padding x , padding y , radius , border , bold flat button padding x , padding y , accent text in the accent color , overlay hover shades what is under it field look box , underline , outline , radius , padding x , padding y check size , radius checkboxes and radio buttons switch look pill , fluent , material ; sliders and radio buttons follow it too slider thumb the knob's radius progress height popup , dialog radius ; dialog also default first OK Cancel and flat buttons focus look : ring a soft ring of the accent or outline a line in the text color, when the keyboard moves the focus A mistake is said when the app starts on the console and by pastel check , with the line: button.height = 40: "button.height" is not a style value . Looks: StyleLookup A style file can have named looks, and a control uses one with StyleLookup as in FireMonkey : Control What a look changes TButton color , hover color , pressed color , text color , border color , border width , radius , padding x , padding y , font size , bold TLabel text color , font size , bold when the label does not set them itself TColumn , TRow , TPanel , TCard ... color , border color , border width , radius when the box does not set them itself TEdit , TMemo , TComboBox , TDatePicker color , border color , border width , radius , padding x , font size A look belongs to a style: when the app uses another style, StyleLookup finds nothing there and the control looks as the style says. A style made on another base = "company" has its looks. pastel check warns about a StyleLookup that no style file in assets/styles/ has. title: Writing components
text: Writing components Like in Delphi, you can add your own components to Pastel. They are used in .pform files and appear in the VS Code designer's toolbox, next to the built in ones. There are two kinds: Kind Examples Base class Registered with Control : drawn on the form, the user sees and uses it a star rating, a date picker, an amount field TControl or a control to build on, like TEdit RegisterControl Non visual component : part of the form, but not drawn a timer, an action, a connection to a service TComponent RegisterNonVisual Complete examples are in examples/components ../examples/components a library with TStarRating and TFormMemory ; TCurrencyEdit and TDatePicker , explained below, are in the framework's pastel.inputs.pas ../framework/src/pastel.inputs.pas and examples/components demo ../examples/components demo an app that uses them . This page explains them step by step. Units and uses : how code finds other code A Pascal unit is one file with a name unit StarRating; . What is in its interface part can be used by other units that name it in their uses list, like use in PHP or import in other languages: Units are found in the project's src/ folder and its sub folders , in the libraries the project depends on, and in the framework Pastel. . For the controls in a .pform file you write no uses : the code Pastel generates for the form names their units. A control of your own writes src/controls/starrating.pas , a working control to change. Every control answers four questions: 1. How big is it? Measure gets the width that is available and gives the size the control wants. The layout rows, columns, Grow , Width / Height in the .pform decides the final size, which is in Bounds when the control is drawn. 2. How does it look? Paint draws inside Bounds with the canvas C see Drawing drawing . Use the colors of Theme , so the control fits the light and the dark theme and assets/theme.toml . 3. What does it do with the mouse and the keyboard? Override what you need: MouseDown X, Y , MouseMove , MouseUp X, Y, Inside , MouseWheel DX, DY , KeyDown Key, Shift, Ctrl return True when the key was used , TextInput S typed text . A control that should get the keyboard focus returns True from Focusable . IsFocused and IsHovered tell its state while painting. 4. What can be set in the .pform and the designer? The published properties and events. They appear in the designer's properties panel, are checked by pastel check , and are set when the form loads: In a setter, call Invalidate when only the look changes Pastel paints that control again and Changed when the size may change layout and paint : Last, register the class at the end of the unit, so .pform files know it: Use it like any control: Saving the unit in VS Code updates the toolbox and the designer's picture: pastel schema , check and preview compile a copy of the pastel tool together with your controls in build/designer/ , again whenever a control changes. Building on an existing control Often a control is an existing one with a little more. TCurrencyEdit is a TEdit with a Value in money: it inherits typing, selection, the clipboard, undo and the look, and adds three things: inherited calls the base class: the control keeps all of TEdit 's behavior and changes only what it overrides. The properties TEdit publishes Text , Placeholder , OnChange ... stay in the designer. A control with a popup TDatePicker shows a date and opens a calendar under itself. The calendar is a TPopup a floating box that closes with Escape or a click outside with a control in it: TPopup.ShowModal Form instead shows it in the middle with the window dimmed and waits until it is closed: that is how Pastel's own dialogs work. TPopup.ShowModal Form, @Done, True does the same without waiting: Done Sender, AResult is called when it is closed, and True frees the popup after that. A popup closed by one of its own buttons is freed with ReleaseLater , after the click is over. A non visual component A component without a

title: Android
text: Android The same Pascal code and .pform forms run on Android phones and tablets. An app is built as libmain.so and packed into an .apk that runs as a NativeActivity : there is no Java code, and Pastel draws the forms itself, as on the desktop. A preview. Building and packing are tested on every change; running is being tried on real phones now. Tell us what you see: an issue with the phone's model and Android version, and the log pastel run target android shows it . Phones, TV boxes and the emulator An Android device has one of four kinds of processor CPU . Pastel builds for all of them, and one .apk can carry all four: Target Android's name Devices Android android arm64 arm64 v8a most phones and tablets since about 2016 5 and newer android arm armeabi v7a older phones, most TV boxes, cheap tablets; 64 bit phones run it too 4.4 and newer android x86 64 x86 64 the Android emulator on a PC Android Studio's, or others 5 and newer android x86 x86 older emulators, a few Intel tablets 4.4 and newer adb shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist tells a device's kind; Settings → About does too on most phones. Setting it up once On Linux Ubuntu, Mint, Debian : pastel doctor install android sets up every kind of device whose binutils assembler and linker are installed, once, into ~/.pastel/ about half a minute : the compilers : the ARM 64 bit one comes with the fpc package; the ARM 32 bit ppcrossarm and x86 ppcross386 ones are built from Free Pascal's sources fpc source — a few seconds each. The 64 bit PC compiler makes x86 64 code itself. Free Pascal's units for Android, for each kind. small stand ins for the phone's system libraries , so the Android NDK is not needed . The third line brings Android's packing tools, a platform android.jar , Java to sign and adb to install on a connected phone or emulator . With Android Studio installed, its SDK is used too ANDROID HOME , or ~/Android/Sdk . pastel setup android does the same and then checks Android's tools one by one Java, the SDK, the platform, the build tools, adb and the phone, bundletool for Google Play and says which commands work; pastel setup android yes installs the missing packages with Android's sdkmanager — Android Studio's, or, when there is none Ubuntu's packages , Google's command line tools fetched into ~/Android/Sdk no sudo . The newest build tools of the SDKs come before older ones on the PATH . pastel doctor then shows ✓ android arm64 , ✓ android arm , ✓ android x86 64 , ✓ android x86 . One kind alone: pastel doctor install android arm . Free Pascal's sources from freepascal.org an archive you unpacked, instead of fpc source work too: point FPCDIR at the folder that has compiler/ and rtl/ in it. Making an app for the phone In VS Code: Pastel: New Project… → Mobile → Android App . Or in a terminal: pastel build target android is android arm64 . pastel package apk puts in every kind this computer is set up for; with platforms = "android arm64", "android arm" in pastel.toml , exactly those. To have it built with the others, add it to the platforms in pastel.toml : Forms for phones phone on pastel new app and pastel new form ; the wizard's Android App uses it, and New Form… in a phone app too makes forms for small, upright screens: the controls are stacked Layout = Flow and as wide as the screen, and edits and buttons are 48 pixels high — the size a finger hits. The designer's size box shows the form at Phone 360 × 640 . A free placed form Layout = Free works on a phone too: give the controls Anchors so they follow the screen's width. In VS Code The status bar shows the platform F9 and Ctrl+F9 use like Delphi's Target Platforms ; a phone app platforms = "android" starts on android . Click it to choose another one. Platform F9 Ctrl+F9 this computer linux , windows build and run build android build for the connected phone's or emulator's CPU, install, start, show the log pastel package apk : one .apk for every kind set up android arm , android x86 64 …

title: The phone's features
text: The phone's features Pastel.Device reaches what a phone has and a desktop program usually does not: the share menu, the phone and browser apps, vibration, notifications, the camera, the place, files from anywhere on the phone — and the permissions some of them need. On Android it uses the phone's own apps and services; on a computer the calls do what makes sense there the browser, the open dialog, desktop notifications or answer that it is not there. Calls that wait for the user These show something of the phone the camera app, the file picker, a permission question and come back when the user is done. The app's window stays alive meanwhile; call them from an event a button's OnClick . Each has a second form that does not wait — shown after these — which is the better way on a phone. Without waiting, the call returns at once and the answer comes to a method of yours — later, never inside the call, also when it is there at once no camera on a computer : Waits Does not wait The method gets TakePhoto TakePhoto @Done Ok , the file PickFile Mime PickFile Mime, @Done Ok , the file GetLocation Place GetLocation @Done Ok , the TPlace RequestPermission P RequestPermission P, @Done Granted TOpenDialog and OpenFileDialog use the same picker on a phone, so code written for the desktop opens files there too. Android A computer ShareText , ShareFile the share menu False LastDeviceError says why OpenUrl the app for the address or file tel: , mailto: , https: , geo: the browser or the file's app Vibrate a buzz nothing Notify the notification bar asks for the permission on Android 13+ the desktop's notifications below notifications PickFile the phone's picker files, Drive, gallery the open dialog TakePhoto the camera app '' GetLocation GPS or the network False RequestPermission asks the user once True PickContact , ReadContacts , AddContact the phone's contacts below contacts and the calendar False AddToCalendar the calendar app, filled in an .ics file in the calendar program ReadCalendar the phone's calendars False SetAppShortcuts the icon's shortcuts below links and the icons shortcuts False EnterPictureInPicture the video in a small window below picture in picture False IsMobile True False Shared with the app Other apps' share menu the gallery, the browser, WhatsApp can list the app. pastel.toml says which kinds it takes; a TShareReceiver controls.md tsharereceiver on the main form gets what was shared — also when the share opened the app: TSharedContent holds Text and Subject a link shared from the browser is its Text , MimeType , and Files : what was shared, copied into the app's cache — one or many photos, a PDF. TakeSharedContent Shared is the same without the component. Links and the icon's shortcuts Links open the app at the right place: from a QR code, a notification, a mail, a web page. pastel.toml lists them, for every platform: A TLinkReceiver controls.md tlinkreceiver on the main form gets the address — also the one that started the app: The app's own scheme shop:// : any link of it opens the app — on Android, and on computers too: the .deb and the Windows installer register the scheme, and the app starts with the address TakeOpenedLink and OnLink find it among the arguments . Its site's addresses https://shop.example.com/app : links under it open the app instead of the browser Android once the site says the app is its own. pastel package apk writes dist/assetlinks.json with the key's fingerprint: put it at https://shop.example.com/.well known/assetlinks.json . An app from Google Play is signed with Play's key: add its fingerprint Play Console → App integrity into the same file. Until then Android shows the link in the browser. The icon's shortcuts come with a long press on the app's icon Android 7.1 and newer and can be dragged to the home screen. Set them at every start they are in the user's language ; a tap opens the app and OnShortcut gets the Id : The icon is a built in icon's name, drawn in the theme's ac

title: Java from Pascal
text: Java from Pascal Android is written in Java: everything a phone can do is a Java class — Toast , AlarmManager , BluetoothAdapter , TextToSpeech , MediaPlayer . Pastel's own units cover what most apps need dialogs, notifications, the camera, the place ; for the rest, Pascal calls Java directly. The classes you need, as Pascal pastel java add reads the classes from Android's android.jar and writes typed Pascal for them into src/java/javaclasses.pas like Delphi's Java2OP : Each class becomes a record named J and the class's name JToast ; an inner class JNotification Builder with: its methods, the inherited ones too, with the same names show , setText , getWidth ; its constructors as New : JIntent.New JavaActivity, ... ; its constants JToast.LENGTH SHORT and static fields JBuild.MODEL . String and CharSequence are Pascal strings; int , long , boolean , double ... their Pascal types; the classes of the list their records; other objects TJavaObject . Java does not keep the names of parameters, so they are named after their types AContext , AInt . A comment above each method shows the Java one. The list is kept in pastel.toml ; pastel java remove takes a class out, pastel java writes the unit again. The file is written by Pastel: change the list, not the file. It is part of the project in git : building does not need Android's SDK. The app's own Java Java files in src/java with their packages' folders are compiled into the app with Pastel's: for an example of Android's documentation copied as it is, or a listener, or anything that is easier in Java. Add their classes to the list like Android's: They need Java's compiler javac , a JDK and Android's d8 build tools 28 or newer or dx . Calls of your own Without the generated records, Pastel.Java calls any method by its name and Java's signature: JavaCall answers nothing; JavaCallZ , ...I , ...J , ...F , ...D , ...O , ...Str a Boolean , Integer , Int64 , Single , Double , TJavaObject , string ; JavaStatic... the same for static methods. Pascal strings become java.lang.String ; objects are passed as Obj.Handle . TJavaObject keeps a Java object alive while Pascal uses it and lets it go by itself, like a string. A Java exception becomes an EJavaError with Java's message: Java calling Pascal: listeners Android tells an app what happened through interfaces: View.OnClickListener , Runnable , TextToSpeech.OnInitListener . JavaImplement makes an object of an interface whose methods are a Pascal method: The handler gets the method's name and its arguments, TJavaObject s: numbers and Boolean s boxed AsInteger , AsInt64 , AsBoolean , AsDouble , strings with AsString . A method that answers sets Answer : an object, a string JavaString , a boxed number of the method's type JavaInteger , JavaInt64 , JavaBoolean , JavaSingle , JavaDouble ; left alone, Java gets null, 0 or False . An exception in the handler becomes a Java RuntimeException where Java called. An interface with two methods of one name onClick View and onClick DialogInterface, int tells them apart with JavaCallbackSignature inside the handler: Java's signature of the method called, ' Landroid/view/View; V' . pastel java add writes Implement for the interfaces of the list; without them, JavaImplement 'android.speech.tts.TextToSpeech$OnInitListener', @SpeechReady . The handler runs on the app's own thread, where forms can be used, like an event of a button: a method that answers nothing void is called later and Java goes on; one that answers waits for it. JavaImplement Name, @Handler, False calls it at once on Java's thread it must not touch forms then . The objects live while the program does: make a listener once, not at each call. Threads Pascal's code runs on the app's own thread; Java can be called from there and from any other thread. Android's views and Toast want Android's UI thread: JavaRunOnUiThread @Method runs a method there, later, without waiting it must not touch Pastel's forms : For a short message ShowToast 'Saved' Pastel.D
headings: The classes you need, as Pascal

title: Console programs
text: Console programs pastel new console mytool creates a command line program that already handles arguments, help and version . This page shows the units that make console programs pleasant to write: Unit For Pastel.Args Options, flags, arguments, sub commands, automatic help Pastel.Term Colors, tables, progress bars, questions Pastel.Text Upper/lower case and lengths that work for every language AppInfo Your program's name and version from pastel.toml generated Arguments: Pastel.Args backup help then prints: Mistakes are explained, with a suggestion when it looks like a typo, and the program ends with exit code 2: Defining arguments Call Flag Name, Short, Help On/off switch: v , verbose . Count tells how often it was given vvv . Option Name, Short, Help, Default Takes a value: o x , ox , o=x , output x , output=x Positional Name, Help A word without a dash, in order. Required unless .Optional or a .Default is set. Command Name, Description A sub command with its own arguments see below Example Line Shown at the end of the help Every definition can be refined by chaining: Method .Default 'x' Value when not given .Required / .Optional Must or need not be given .Many Option: may be given several times. Positional: takes all remaining words. .IsInteger , .IntRange 1, 9 Must be a whole number in a range .Choices 'a', 'b' Must be one of these .Env 'NAME' Taken from this environment variable when not on the command line .MetaVar 'FILE' Placeholder shown in the help Short names are one letter; use '' for none. ends the options, so tool file passes file as a word. Reading values Args.Has 'verbose' Was it given? Defaults do not count. Args.Get 'output' The value, or the default Args.GetInt 'level' The value as a number Args.GetAll 'exclude' All values of a .Many option or positional Args.Count 'verbose' How many times a flag was given Sub commands todo help lists the commands; todo add help shows the options of add . Terminal: Pastel.Term Colors: Bold , Dim , Italic , Underline , Red , Green , Yellow , Blue , Magenta , Cyan , Gray , and Rgb ' 4F46E5', Text . They switch themselves off when the output goes to a file or a pipe, when NO COLOR is set, or with no color . FORCE COLOR=1 keeps them on. Tables Columns line up with colored text and with letters like ş or 漢 . Progress In a terminal it is one updating line: 45% 45/100 copying . In a log file it writes a line every 10%. Questions Confirm accepts y/yes and n/no also e/evet, h/hayır . Questions read from standard input, so answers can be piped in for scripts and tests: printf 'Ali\ny\n' mytool . IsInteractive tells whether someone is there to answer. Text: Pastel.Text Free Pascal's UpperCase and LowerCase only change A–Z, and Length counts bytes. For text in any language use: Upper 'ayşe' 'AYŞE' Upper 'istanbul', 'tr' 'İSTANBUL' Turkish and Azerbaijani dotted i: 'tr' , 'az' Lower 'ILIK', 'tr' 'ılık' Capitalize 'şehir' 'Şehir' CharCount 'ağaç' 4 Length gives 6 CharCopy 'ağaç', 2, 2 'ğa' Shorten 'çok uzun bir yazı', 7 'çok uz…' Program information: AppInfo Pastel generates the unit AppInfo from pastel.toml on every build: Change version in pastel.toml and version follows. UTF 8 and threads Pastel adds a small start up unit to every program: All text is UTF 8 on every platform. On Windows the console is switched to UTF 8 too, so WriteLn 'Çiğdem' and arguments like mytool ayşe work as on Linux. Threads work right away. With plain Free Pascal on Linux, cthreads has to be the first unit in the program's uses , or TThread stops the program with "no thread support".

title: JSON, settings and logging
text: JSON, settings and logging Three units that every service and most tools need: Unit For Pastel.Json Reading and writing JSON, objects to JSON and back Pastel.Config Settings from files, environment variables and code Pastel.Log Log messages to the console, journald, files or log collectors JSON: Pastel.Json Reading JStr , JInt , JFloat , JBool Data, Path, Default A value by path, or the default when it is missing or of another kind. Text like "12" or "yes" is converted. JArray Data, Path The items of an array they belong to Data : do not free them JHas Data, Path , JFind Data, Path Is it there / the raw TJSONData ParseJson Text , LoadJsonFile Name Comments // and trailing commas are allowed A mistake in the text raises EJsonError with the line and column: config.json, line 4, column 12: Unexpected token . Writing JObject takes names and values in turn. Values can be text, numbers, booleans, nil null , and other TJSONData which JObject then owns . Objects Classes with published properties convert in both directions: The types are Free Pascal's own TJSONData , TJSONObject and TJSONArray from fpjson, so everything fpjson offers works too. Settings: Pastel.Config with a config.toml like: Where settings come from The later source wins: 1. SetDefault in code 2. the system file: /etc/myapp/config.toml Windows: %ProgramData%\myapp\config.toml 3. the user's file: ~/.config/myapp/config.toml Windows: %APPDATA%\myapp\config.toml 4. ./config.toml or config.json in the current folder 5. environment variables: MYAPP SERVER PORT for server.port , MYAPP DATABASE PASSWORD for database.password 6. SetValue in code, for example from a command line option LoadStandard loads 2–5. For other set ups use LoadFile , LoadFileIfExists and LoadEnv Prefix in the order you want. Files can be TOML or JSON. Environment variables are the usual way to give secrets to a service systemd Environment= , Docker e , so they never have to be written in a file. Reading Get Key, Default Text GetInt , GetFloat , GetBool Typed values; GetBool accepts true/false, yes/no, on/off, 1/0 GetList Key A TOML/JSON array, or comma separated text MYAPP ADMINS="ali, ayşe" Has Key Is it set anywhere? Require Key The value, or an error that says how to set it Source Key Where the value came from Files The files that were loaded Errors say exactly what is wrong and where: Logging: Pastel.Log Messages go to standard error: Level Log.Level := llDebug or llInfo , the default, llWarn , llError , llOff . Log.SetLevel 'debug' takes the name, handy with a setting or option. Every Pastel program also reads the environment variable LOG LEVEL : LOG LEVEL=debug ./myapp . Formats Log.Format lfAuto default Text in a terminal; journald format when the program runs under systemd lfText time LEVEL message name=value lfJournal <3 message with the syslog priority, no time journald adds it lfJson One JSON object per line: {"time":"...Z","level":"info","msg":"...","user":"ali"} With the journald format, journalctl u myapp p err shows only errors. Files Old files are named app.log.1 newest to app.log.5 . Under systemd, logging to the journal is usually all you need. Threads Logging is safe from several threads at once; lines are never mixed.

title: Reports, PDF, Excel and printing
text: Reports, PDF, Excel and printing Business programs hand out paper: invoices, receipts, lists, exports for the accountant. Pastel makes them without other programs or libraries, in desktop apps, services and command line tools alike: Unit For Pastel.Report reports Invoices, lists, letters: headings, text, tables and totals that flow over pages; PDF or HTML Pastel.Pdf pdf pages drawn by you PDF pages drawn by you: text, lines, boxes, pictures at exact places labels, forms, receipts Pastel.Sheets excel and csv Excel files .xlsx and CSV, written and read Pastel.Xml xml XML for other programs e invoices, exports Pastel.Print printing and opening The printers, printing a file, opening it in the system's viewer The salon example ../examples/salon desk/README.md uses all of them: its invoices as PDF, printed, as an Excel list — on the desktop and from its server. Reports Everything is written from top to bottom; when the page is full, a new one starts, and a table repeats its heads on it. Title S , Heading S A big title; a smaller bold heading Text S, Align , Note S A paragraph long lines wrap; paLeft , paCenter , paRight ; smaller grey text Fields Name, Value, ... Names and values in two columns Table Heads, Widths, Aligns , Row Cells, Bold , EndTable Widths in millimetres, 0 shares what is left; aligns as letters: L , R , C . Cells wrap Total Name, Value, Bold Sums at the right Image File, Width, Align , Rule , Space Mm , NewPage A picture PNG or JPEG , a thin line, empty space, a page break Footer , Header , Logo On every page {page} , {pages} , on pages after the first, on the first TextSize , Accent , Striped , Margin Size of text 10 pt , the color of titles and table heads, striped rows, the margin 18 mm SaveToFile , ToBytes , ToHtml .pdf or .html ; the PDF as bytes web, e mail ; the HTML page Pdf , Y , OnNewPage The page under it, for drawing of your own at Y ; a method called on every new page Letters. Text uses a TrueType font of the system DejaVu Sans or Liberation Sans on Linux, Arial on Windows , or assets/fonts/Regular.ttf and Bold.ttf of your app, or PASTEL FONT . Only the letters that are used go into the file, so an invoice of one page is around 30 KB, and every letter — ş, ğ, İ, €, ₺ — prints right everywhere. On a server , the same report answers a request: PDF: pages drawn by you For things that must sit at exact places — labels, a form to fill in, a receipt — draw the page yourself. Positions are millimetres from the top left corner. Text X, Y, S , TextAligned X, Y, W, S, Align , TextBox X, Y, W, S, Align Text with its top at Y; in a box W wide; wrapped returns its height TextWidth S , LineHeight , WrapText S, W Measuring Line X1, Y1, X2, Y2 , Rect X, Y, W, H, Fill, Stroke , Image X, Y, W, H, File Shapes and pictures SetFont Size, Bold , TextColor , FillColor , StrokeColor , LineWidth Colors as ' RRGGBB' , widths in millimetres NewPage , SetPage I , PageCount , PageWidth , PageHeight Pages LoadFonts Regular, Bold Other .ttf files Title , Author , Subject Shown by PDF viewers Excel and CSV Numbers, dates TDateTime and True / False go into Excel as such, so it can sum and sort them; everything else is text. ToBytes gives the file for a web answer Res.Bytes S.ToBytes, 'application/vnd.openxmlformats officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet', 'invoices.xlsx' . Reading: Numbers come as text with a dot '1380.6' , dates as Excel's day numbers 46329 = 3 November 2026; TDateTime counts the same way . CSV: ReadCsv File guesses the separator , , ; or tab and understands quotes; WriteCsv File, Rows, ';' writes what Excel opens right with a UTF 8 mark; ; where Excel expects it, in countries that write 1,5 . ParseCsv Text and CsvText Rows work on text. XML Texts and attributes are escaped & , < , quotes ; a missing Close is an error. To read XML, Free Pascal's DOM and XMLRead units are there: ReadXMLFile Doc, 'file.xml' . Printing and opening Printers , DefaultPrinter The names of the printers PrintFile File, Printer,

title: Files, programs, HTTP and the environment
text: Files, programs, HTTP and the environment Unit For Pastel.Files Reading and writing files, folders, paths, sizes Pastel.Process Running other programs and reading their output Pastel.Http HTTP and HTTPS requests, JSON APIs, downloads Pastel.Env Environment variables in UTF 8 on every system All text is UTF 8, and errors say in plain words what went wrong and with which file, program or address. Files: Pastel.Files WriteText never leaves a half written file: it writes a temporary file and puts it in place at the end, so a crash or a full disk keeps the old content. ReadText , WriteText , AppendText Whole files as text a UTF 8 byte order mark is dropped ReadLines , WriteLines Line by line ReadBytes , WriteBytes Binary data TBytes ListFiles Dir, Pattern, Recursive Full paths, sorted ListDirs Dir Sub folders, sorted EnsureDir Dir Creates the folder and its parents CopyFile Src, Dest , MoveFile Src, Dest Create the destination folder; keep the time of the file DeleteFileIfExists Name , DeleteDir Dir DeleteDir removes everything inside FileSize , FileModified JoinPath 'data', 'users', 'ali.json' With / or \ for the system RelativePath File, BaseDir AppDir , HomeDir , MakeTempDir The program's folder, the user's folder, a new empty temporary folder FormatSize 1536 '1.5 KB' Errors raise EFileError : cannot read "config.txt": cannot open it does it exist, and may this program read it? . Programs: Pastel.Process Arguments are passed exactly as given, one by one: spaces, quotes, and $ need no escaping and are not interpreted. Only Shell goes through the system shell /bin/sh , or cmd.exe on Windows for pipes, wildcards and redirections. Run Exe, Args Waits, returns TRunResult RunOutput Exe, Args The output without the last line break; raises EProcessError with the program's error text when it fails RunLive Exe, Args Shares this program's terminal, returns the exit code Shell CommandLine Like Run , through the shell Which Name Full path of a program on PATH , or '' TRunResult has ExitCode , Output , Errors , TimedOut , Duration ms , Ok , Text the output without the final line break and Lines . Options: A failure reads like "git" failed exit code 128 : fatal: not a git repository . A missing program: program "ffmpeg" was not found is it installed and on PATH? . HTTP: Pastel.Http For an API you call often, use a client: THttpClient Get Path , Get Path, Query , Head , Delete Post , Put , Patch Path, Body, ContentType PostJson , PutJson Path, Json Text or a TJSONData PostForm Path, 'name', 'value', ... Like an HTML form Request Method, Path, Body, ContentType Any method Download Path, FileName Streams to the file; nothing is left behind when it fails BaseUrl , Headers , BearerToken , UserName / Password Sent with every request Timeout Milliseconds for connecting and for each read default 30000 FollowRedirects Default on OnProgress procedure Done, Total: Int64 while the answer arrives Proxy 'http://host:port' , or 'none' THttpResponse has Status , StatusText , Body , Headers , Url after redirects , Duration , and: Ok : status 200–299. Error statuses 404, 500, … are normal answers, not exceptions. Header 'content type' : a header by name, any case. Json : the body parsed you free it . RaiseForStatus : EHttpError unless Ok , with the start of the body: GET https://api.example.com/x: 404 Not Found: no such user . When no answer comes at all, EHttpError says why: HTTPS Certificates are checked, including that they belong to the host name, just like a browser. Free Pascal 3.2.2 on its own does not do this, nor does it find OpenSSL 3 what current Linux systems ship or go through a proxy for HTTPS; Pastel.Http takes care of all three. Linux : needs libssl3 or 1.1 , installed on nearly every system. pastel doctor checks it. Windows : nothing to install: Pastel.Http uses Windows' own HTTP WinINet , with Windows' certificates and proxy settings. PASTEL HTTP=fpc uses Free Pascal's instead, which needs libssl 3 x64.dll , libcrypto 3 x64.dll and cacert.
